speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister who, on September 4, told the House that the government intended to move ahead with an oil pipeline to Montreal. That is about four months ago. Can the Prime Minister tell the House precisely what is holding up the commencement of this project or holding up an application being made to the National Energy Board, which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources yesterday said might be made in the spring? Why is this whole project still in the discussion stage after four months?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the minister also indicated yesterday
Oral Questions
that he expects to be able to announce a decision very soon. I want to repeat that assurance to the House. The hold-up, to use the expression of the Leader of the Opposition, is due to the fact that we have tried to ascertain provincial preferences as to alternate routes, alternate ways of laying down the pipeline. In the meantime we have proceeded, as the House knows, through the Canadian Commercial Corporation with regard to the guarantee that there would be a supply of pipe. For that reason we are still confident that the deadline I announced will be met.

subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: The Prime Minister spoke about consulting with the provinces about the route. Can he indicate what provinces the government is consulting about the route and what provinces, if any, the government is consulting about the size of the pipeline and the volume of oil to be carried through the pipeline?

subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, consultations have been mainly with Ontario and Quebec. There may have been other consultations but I know of those two in particular. We have ascertained, in the case of Quebec, what appears to be a slight preference for one route over another. In the case of Ontario, they have refused, I understand, to indicate a preference for one route over another.

subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: Has the government of Canada reached any understanding or agreement with the government of Quebec about the size of the Quebec market for oil or the volume of the oil used in Quebec that would be dedicated to Canadian crude? In other words, has the government of Canada consulted the government of Quebec about the amount of Canadian crude which would be dedicated to the Quebec market, and have any discussions taken place with the Atlantic provinces in this respect?

subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so far as I know the discussions have been general. The question is not only one of the amount of crude but of the time over which such various amounts would be deliverable in the eastern market. With regard to consultation with the Atlantic provinces, I would have to defer on this matter to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who has been, of course, closer to it than I have been.

subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-REASON FOR DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT-THROUGHPUT VOLUME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize, but may I direct one further supplementary question either to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Is the decision to supply roughly 250,000 barrels a day to those markets in the east based upon consultations with the eastern provinces, or is it based upon some other consideration because, of course, 250,000 barrels a day would constitute only about one-quarter of the market of those five eastern provinces and therefore would offer the prospect of supplying only about one-quarter of the market?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, January 7, consideration of Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian Nation-

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
al Railways system and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June, 1974, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and motions Nos. 1 and 2 (Mr. Blenkarn).

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, transportation is becoming more important to development in Canada, and as its form changes obviously the attitude of Canadians to transportation will have to progress with the times. Last evening I mentioned that Canadians now have a chance to take a new direction with respect to the development of rail transportation, following the retirement of the President of Canadian National Railways after a long and faithful career devoted to the railroad industry. In appointing a new president I hope the government will keep in mind the opportunities now existing to develop a new direction for Canadian National.
The two amending motions before us suggest that extra money be made available for transportation. One of the sacrifices I suggest is CN Tower Limited, which is building a most prestigious tower surpassing in size and height everything else in the city of Toronto, and the purpose of which is reported to be the installation of an antenna to allow better communications to be undertaken by Canadian National.
I am in agreement with those who say that the fundamental responsibility of Canadian National is to operate transportation facilities, and that less attention should be paid to the fringe elements which, rightly or wrongly, Canadian National has accumulated in its portfolio over the years. As a matter of fact, the only changes made in the transportation system have been disadvantageous. We are now providing service to fewer rail passengers and will be encountering immediate difficulties in transporting freight. Allowing Canadian National to continue expenditures in fields other than transportation is not in the interests of transportation as it should develop in Canada within the next decade.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has just mentioned the fact that Canadian National has been operating two trains out of Toronto one minute apart. If there is anything more idiotic than that, I have yet to hear of it. It might be more advantageous to use two engines and twice as many cars in one train. We do not use one engine with ten boxcars on a freight train, and then five minutes later send out another train with as many boxcars. We have used as many as five engines and 220 boxcars. It seems to me that this would be the logical way to operate a passenger service. The discussions that have taken place have amply demonstrated that the management of Canadian National is not seriously considering the problems that we have with transportation and is not doing anything about them.
It is interesting to note that a number of hon. members have voted for a safety report that was specially commissioned. It is also interesting to recall that the former member for Moose Jaw, John Skoberg, continually pointed

out that these safety regulations were being violated. Solutions were offered to most of the safety problems encountered by the Canadian National and other railways. These problems are well known; they are certainly well known to the people who work on the railroads. I think they are also known to everyone connected with safety in both the Canadian Safety Association and the provincial associations. Now, we have a study which again indicates that changes have to take place before we can develop a modern, up-to-date and viable transportation facility. It is, therefore, necessary to consider the amendments that are before us in terms of whether they help in providing a transportation facility. It is my opinion that they do not. They may produce some effect on the communication facility, but they do not provide any type of facility that will assist in the transportation arrangements in this nation. One wonders if money saved in that field could be better used in other fields.
I have no quarrel with the Canadian National building the Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal. The station is in the basement and there are complete services in the hotel for the travelling public, some of whom arrive by train. But this parliament allowed the stupid mistake-one that I tried to prevent-of moving the rail facilities from downtown Ottawa. The late Alex Caron and I should probably have our names engraved on the Convention Centre which used to be Union Station because that is all we were able to salvage from the old railway station. If we had trains arriving in downtown Ottawa and downtown Montreal today, we obviously would not be considering STOL aircraft flying from Rockcliffe to Ste. Helene Island in Montreal in order to provide rapid transit. This would have been provided by rail had the railway station not been moved four or five miles away from the core of Ottawa while the Montreal station remained in the core of the city. It may be to our advantage to keep the downtown core connected by rapid transit and the best way to do that may be to maintain facilities in the core of cities. But the CNR towers in Toronto do not accomplish that; they are not providing that type of facility and there is no indication that the employees of the business offices in the towers will use rail transportation. The railroad is obviously not going to move from Union Station to the CNR tower in Toronto. That is a prestigous office building which involves the investment portfolio of the Canadian National Railways but it does not provide a transportation facility.
If the government is wise in its appointment of a new president for the Canadian National Railways we will be looking at rapid ground transportation into the high Arctic, as well as in the east and in the west, and the provision of transportation to meet the needs of the people of this country, rather than a CNR tower.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few brief remarks in support of the amendment presently before this House which was proposed by the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn). It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that this piece of legislation is before us under these particular circumstances, indicates some rather poor administrative and legislative procedures in the government's handling of this important
January 8, 1974

question of the financing of Canada's major Crown corporation.
The major difficulty which gives rise to some of the spirit-and as far as that goes, the basis for the fact that members have found it necessary to make amendments to this bill-is, as the hon. member for Mississauga has pointed out, that the CNR has abandoned to a large extent its primary function. This point has also been made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and other members who have preceded me in this debate.
The difficulty in which this House finds itself when discussing this important piece of legislation was precipitated, I suggest with deference, Mr. Speaker, by the unusual and somewhat reprehensible practice followed by the present head of the CTC, when he was a minister in this place, of interrupting the established procedure for the appointment of auditors. We now have the rather ridiculous situation where we have one auditor coming, one auditor going, one auditor gone and two auditors hanging on. We have the firm of Cooper and Lybrands which is going to be entrusted with auditing the CN for the next few years as the result of an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming which was accepted in committee and now forms part of the bill. It was a good amendment because it gave a little stability to a precarious situation. At one stage we had a situation where a firm of auditors had been appointed approximately for 40 years, and then were discharged. This made it most difficult to have an annual report submitted because those auditors enjoyed the so-called sanctity of parliamentary approval, while their successors have not received it.
In the last session of this parliament the government introduced the predecessor of this bill, the Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act, 1971. That bill covered the financing period from January 1,
1971	to June 30, 1972. The government brought the bill on for second reading on March 6, 1972 and on April 21, 1972 the debate on second reading was adjourned. The government never proceeded with the bill during the life of that parliament. This indicates the respect they must have for this particular piece of legislation.
In this session, Your Honour, the government introduced Bill C-164 on March 19, 1973, which relates to the financing period of January 1, 1973 to June 30, 1974. The only retroactive provision with respect to the year 1972 appears in clause 13, but it is not adequately set out. In effect, we now have a bill covering the CNR and Air Canada financing for the period from January 1, 1971 to June 30, 1974, a 3V& year period. There is a six-months hiatus not covered by the bills that extends from July 1,
1972	to December 31, 1972.
It is obvious that neither the ministry of transport nor the government are treating this legislation with the respect it deserves. It is equally obvious that the financial affairs of CN and Air Canada are controlled by the government alone. The annual financing bill in many respects is a mockery. It is designed to delude the public and its representatives in this House into thinking that they control these two great and important public utilities.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
In essence, the CNR has only to give the government a promissory note for whatever hundreds of millions of taxpayers' money it wants. And, if Air Canada wants any money, it can include that sum in the amount on the face of its promissory note. I, therefore, think that Parliament should be more selective in approving and authorizing funds. That, of course, is the spirit and intent behind the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Mississauga.
It is obvious that CNR has neglected its primary function, that of moving goods and services efficiently. Canadian National, in particular, needs to modernize its transportation capabilities. The current energy crisis has shown that in this country we are not fully capable of coping with this situation from the point of view of transportation. I am sure that is apparent to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Unfortunately, the situation of CN has become so critical that nothing can be done over the short term. Ironically, the energy crisis may bring about the development and improvement of the Canadian National system. This sort of thing appears to be happening in the United States. According to a recent article in the Wall Street Journal, the energy crisis will cause an extended use of Amtrack. Clearly, it is in the interest of the United States to improve the capability of its railways, and that system is an experiment in that direction. What is Canada doing?
Both the present Minister of Transport and his predecessor in office have said repeatedly that the CN financial structure, as well as transport policies, are in desperate need of revision and modernization. The fact that the schedule of the Rapido train was changed without the knowledge of the Minister of Transport shows that there is a lack of direction with regard to that major utility. The fact that the President of Air Canada did not know about the proposed airport head tax until he read about it in the newspapers indicates a lack of consultation. It is obvious to anyone speaking to top executives of Air Canada, as well as other air line and CN employees, that there are morale problems. That this situation has been allowed to develop is an indictment of this government.
The situation was much the same under the former minister of transport. In March, 1972, as recorded at page 808 of Hansard, he said:
I agree with the claim that a reorganized structure is necessary in order that members and the country generally can obtain more information, and obtain it more easily, about all aspects of transportation. With this objective in mind, I propose to bring before the House in the next session three important pieces of legislation on which work is proceeding at the present time.
Remember, that was said in March, 1972. I continue:
The first of those is a bill designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, thus divorcing it, as it were, from the CNR. I will also introduce a Canadian National Railways revision act and a companion piece of legislation covering amendments to the Railway Act. Hon. members will know how involved and far reaching these changes are; they have been asking for them for the last two or three years.
Following the commitment given by the former minister of transport, the present minister has been making announcements and promises. Unfortunately, there has not been action. The minister knows how desirable it is to move passengers quickly and efficiently between major

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada eastern Canadian cities and other centres. I suggest, in all seriousness, that it would be sensible to do as the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) suggested last night, divert some of the funds slated for the airport at Pickering and for the STOL experiment, to the Canadian National, in order to enable the railway to construct a modern and efficient roadbed which would permit passengers and goods to be moved at speeds between 100 and 125 miles per hour from one eastern Canadian city to another. This would be of great benefit to us all. Professor Lukasiewicz of Carleton University has suggested that the standard of Canadian transportation lags very badly behind that of other modern countries in the world. While modern western industrial nations are placing increasing emphasis on improving their public transport systems, Canada is doing the reverse.
Canadian National Railways, as the hon. member for Mississauga suggested yesterday, is entering the hotel business to an ever increasing extent. In addition, it is acquiring expensive real estate, building a tower, and is involved in 38 subsidiary enterprises some of which are not related to, or collateral to except under the loosest definitions, the business of transport by rail. The company is more interested in doing these things than in fulfilling the kind of role which Canadians have a right to expect it to fulfil.
Britain at present is testing an electric train, or a diesel electric train which can go 130 miles an hour. Research and development in the Canadian National company in this area has been pitiful, as is evident if one looks at the work entitled "Institutionalization of Canadian Rail Obsolescence", by Professor Lukasiewicz.
It was apparent, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) suggested, that officials of Canadian National and Air Canada were not overly frank with the committee. They were reluctant to tell us of the duties of top management officials, although the committee did learn about collateral ventures in which the railway was engaged. Information which the committee justifiably required was not always forthcoming. In examining the basis on which the officials of these companies had refused to divulge information, I learned that a similar problem had arisen in the U.K. in connection with select committees. In this may I read from May's Eighteenth Edition, page 654. This paragraph deals with "select committee on nationalized industries" and reads:
A demand for some new parliamentary machinery to scrutinize the activities of those industries and services transferred to public ownership after the second world war ...
There is little difference between a nationalized industry in the U.K. and a Canadian Crown corporation such as Air Canada or the CNR. Although I cannot quote in detail reports regarding the activities of the committee in question, it is said on page 655:
For the first decade of its existence the Committee investigated on average one nationalized industry each session. In 1966-67 the membership of the Committee was increased and since then the Committee has conducted its enquiries by means of sub-committees either examining two subjects concurrently or else separate aspects of one industry.
If it were permitted under the rules, we should make an effort to follow this practice and procedure in the Canadian parliament, so that Crown agencies such as Air Canada and the CNR could be more accountable to the public. It is
[Mr. MacKay.l
obvious from the committee proceedings that the trend is for the bureaucrats in these Crown corporations to proceed further and further away from their primary roles. It must be obvious at this time that the people of Canada have a right to expect better performance from their major Crown corporations. When answering a question today, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made reference to the fact that Air Canada was an hour late. Everyone laughed because this is what we have come to expect.
If we look at the record of the scheduling of Canadian National Railways, we see that it is a terrible record wreck. Most of the time they will not even guarantee that a passenger will arrive at a particular time. It appears their attitude is they will sell someone a ticket and he will have to take his chances on when he will get there. Canadians have a right to expect something better than that.
With regard to the need for secrecy as to what these Crown corporations are doing, the activities of their main executive officers, how much they are paid, on what basis they were appointed and so on, this is something the people of Canada are interested in knowing. To say that divulging this information would somehow prejudice the operations of these enterprises is patently ridiculous. If they are of any value, they should be paid the going rate. If they are paid something less than that or are merely redundant and have positions that are not necessary for the operations of Air Canada or CNR, they should be removed.
It would be very interesting for the committee and the House of Commons to know on what basis the continuation of the present situation exists whereby Air Canada and CNR are still intertwined in their directorship. It would be interesting to know why this venture into the Canadian aerospace industry was initiated by the officials of Air Canada. It would be interesting to check further into the Wardair situation. Each time members of this House attempted in Committee to find out why these things were done, whose idea it was, whether guidance was given from the minister or on what particular basis the directors or officials proceeded, we were told, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said, that the confidentiality of the matter precluded answering this type of question.
As far as CNR is concerned, I do not see why it should be permitted to continue to expect the people of Canada to provide funds for ventures like the CN tower until it has decided to proceed with its primary role of moving people and freight for the benefit of Canadians. There was never a time in this country when commodities were in such short supply in various parts of the nation. We have a feed grain shortage in eastern Canada. The British Columbia apple industry and lumber industry are cramped because of a lack of adequate rail facilities. The problems involved in moving wheat are well known.
I had a little difficulty last night following the logic of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). I do not want to misquote him. I think he said that CN wanted to build this tower because CP has one in Calgary. He pointed out that he did not think this was necessarily a
January 8, 1974

good thing because the customers of CP had to pay for it. If it is not a good thing for CP, I fail to see why it should be a good thing for CN, even though it is a Crown corporation.
In any event, it seems clear that the principles involved in the amendments of the hon. member for Mississauga deserve support by all members of this House for the simple reason they are an indication that parliament is master of the activities of CNR and Air Canada. It would indicate the parliament of Canada does not approve of so much emphasis being placed on collateral activities such as hotels, towers and this type of thing, the cost of which should be scrutinized and deleted from the estimates for the calendar year 1973. Let these projects be financed, if they are necessary strictly from internal earnings. The fact that this direction is given by Parliament will be an indication to the officials of CNR that parliament is disturbed, and rightly so, about their activities in fields not directly related to transport. It should be a warning to Mr. MacMillan who indicated that intermodal methodology of handling business is a good thing. I do not know what he meant exactly by "intermodal methodology," but that is what he said in one of his answers in committee. As far as the Canadian parliament is concerned, intermodal methodology by C.N.R. should be confined to moving freight and moving people, not building towers and hotels.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke in the debate when this bill was before the House for second reading on April 13. At that time I referred to the bill as an exercise in futility and an affront to this parliament. Nothing that has transpired since that time has altered my opinion of the bill. In fact, events since that date have served to buttress my opinion and reaffirm my conviction that this government, as it does from time with the CNR financing bill, is again playing games with this House.
This bill is a ridiculous exercise. I hesitated to speak on it again because I have spoken so often on similar bills over the past five years that I am beginning to wonder if there is any way of getting through to this government. I thought I would try once more to convince the government they should at least heed some of the advice of their own cabinet ministers who have said over and over again that this is a bad form of legislation, that there is no proper control over the financing of these two corporations and a new method of financing should be introduced. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) read some statements by previous Ministers of Transport and the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) promising that legislation would be forthcoming to provide financing for these two Crown corporations in such a way that parliament would have some control over their spending, which in aggregate has been hundreds of millions of dollars every year.
This is a good time to look at the history of these financing bills. I say that because whether we agree wholeheartedly with the principle of the amendments, it is simply to bring before this House the fact that CN and Air Canada have grown beyond parliament. They have gone beyond the priorities that were set for them when they were formed many years ago. They have certainly gone beyond the priorities established for them in the National
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada Transportation Act. It is time to examine what has happened since Bill C-164 was introduced to determine to what extent parliament is being bypassed by CNR and Air Canada.
Members on both sides have heard the comments made in the House by various ministers that new legislation would be brought down. They have attended meetings of the committee and heard witnesses dodge questions which were put to them, withhold complete answers, hide behind the cloak of confidentiality and in other ways avoid giving true answers to members of parliament. The presence on the order paper of amendments of the type we are considering is a good reflection of what went on in committee, and the way members on this side feel about the type of financing bill we are being asked to pass.
Bill C-164 was given first reading on March 19, and second reading on April 13 and 16. Twelve speakers took part in the debate at that time. Yet despite the government's assertions that this is an important piece of legislation the bill was set aside for six months and was not considered again until October 18 at which time there were five days of debate during which 46 speakers took part. Surely, we cannot accept the contention of the government that we have been delaying important legislation when 46 members feel obliged to say something about the operations of the two corporations concerned, as, of course, they are entitled to do.
Once the bill went to committee, it was handled very expeditiously in my opinion. The committee met on November 8, held 12 sittings and heard a number of witnesses. It reported back on December 20. I have described the bill as an exercise in futility but I would modify that opinion to this extent-it is an excellent vehicle for securing the attendance of officials of the CN and Air Canada before the committee. It gave us an opportunity to put questions to them which we had raised without success in the House. On each occasion the minister had sidetracked them in the usual way by saying he would take them up with the CN or Air Canada.
Perhaps the best witness I can call in support of my view that we are being asked to conduct an exercise in futility is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who also appeared before the committee. Someone asked him directly why the bill was necessary. He said, in effect, that if the bill were not passed the CN and Air Canada would have to borrow money on the commercial market and pay more for it. After all, the legislation before us is not necessary to enable those companies to borrow money. They already have that power under existing statutes. The minister added that the bill was necessary, too, because it gave parliament control over the appointment of auditors. One of my hon. friends has shown how little control parliament does, in fact, exercise over the appointment of auditors. The minister himself admitted that this appointment to the result of a cabinet decision taken without consultation and slipped into the bill for approval by parliament later. This is the way in which the government effectively bypasses the section of the act which says parliament must appoint the auditor each year.

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
The frustration which boils up regularly in this chamber is nothing new. It appears every time a financing bill comes before the House. It is felt not only by members of the opposition. Objection to this type of financing is also taken by cabinet ministers, by a previous minister of transport and by other responsible members of the government. I recall questions being directed to the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), then Minister of Transport, when one of these bills was before the House back in 1971. We were complaining about the fact that so many of the expenditures outlined in the bill had already been made. Since there was nothing we could do about them, what was the point of discussing them?
On this point, I should like to quote from the committee report, issue No. 1. of the third session of the 28th Parliament. We were questioning the Minister of Transport of that day about the desirability of this type of legislation. He said:
This is really to permit them (the CNR) during 1971 to cover commitments made prior to that time.
He went on to say:
It is not an entirely satisfactory system from the standpoint of the committee or I may say from the standpoint of the government. I have been saying to both these corporations that they should really adopt a further forward forecasting mechanism and I have been trying to get both of them on a five-year forecasting period ... As I say, I agree with you that it is not a very satisfactory way of doing things because in a sense we are really approving something of which a good deal has already been done.
Later, I asked the minister a further question, to which he replied:
I do not want to take the responsibility for something which has been embedded in the system for decades, really, but nevertheless it is something which in my judgment we ought to get rid of or improve in some way so that we do not find ourselves in this kind of situation involving, in a way, an after-the-fact judgment.
This is what we have been complaining about. What is the point of spending days and weeks questioning officials in committee when, in fact, the money has all been spent and there is nothing one can do about it? Yet despite the views expressed by the then Minister of Transport and the promises he made in the House, nothing has been done to change the situation.
When the present bill was before the committee, I questioned the Minister of Finance about this method of financing. As members will see if they turn to issue No. 19 of the committee proceedings in the first session of the 29th Parliament, I asked him, as reported on page 25, whether he agreed that this was a proper way to finance large corporations. He replied:
No, I think it is not a satisfactory way, Mr. Thomas. I think these bills are important enough to be dealt with expeditiously by Parliament.
In reply to a further question I put to him, the Minister of Finance said:
I agree with Mr. Thomas, Mr. Chairman. I think we have to develop some more permanent mechanism for the financing of these two corporations while allowing for parliamentary control either by way of the Department of Transport estimates or through some other mechanism. I agree this is not a satisfactory procedure.
I do not know what further evidence the government needs. If they will not listen to us on this side of the House complaining that parliament is being bypassed or ignored,

surely they will listen to the brains on that side. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) all agree that this is bad legislation, that parliament has been bypassed. Since they continue to bring in the same type of legislation, hon. members should not wonder why I claim that the government is deliberately mocking this House and affronting our intelligence. This is the kind of thing that leads to amendments of this nature.
There is a feeling among members of parliament that the CNR and Air Canada are going on in their own merry way and have forgotten the primary purpose of their incorporation. The CN was designed to run a railway. Air Canada was designed to fly aeroplanes. Yet we have no control over these corporations or can give them no direction as to how they spend their money, so naturally we should not be prepared to accept this kind of legislation. In fact, I contend that if parliament is to retain any control over the spending of these two corporations, some definite changes must be made in the financing of CN and Air Canada. I suggest that much of the mess we are in now began with the National Transportation Act of 1967. I was not here at that time, but I understand what parliament was trying to do. Although the act was viable and satisfactory in the conditions prevailing at that time, it is becoming more obvious every day that the conditions which applied in 1967 no longer apply today.
When the act was passed in 1967, it was felt that transportation should be placed on a profit making basis, or at least on a compensatory basis. The railways were instructed to make a profit, and this accounts for some of the difficulties today. Members of this House rise and fire broadsides at the CN, but in all honesty the CN is only doing what the House instructed it to do by statute. As a result, we now face an almost insurmountable obstacle: we have given the CN instructions to do just what it is doing today. We have told CN to go out and make money and not to worry about giving service.
I suggest that we are not going to change the situation by lambasting the CNR and Air Canada. Let us put the blame where it belongs, that is on ministers who have said that the whole set-up at the moment is wrong. Let them back up their words by bringing in legislation to correct the situation. I suggest they start by bringing in amendments to the National Transportation Act, which would provide some method whereby the government could tell CN and Air Canada just what their priorities are, and that we do not want them building hotels and towers until and unless they provide a proper freight and passenger train service in this country.
There are many priorities that some body should be laying down for both the CNR and Air Canada. I do not want to go into the details here since I do not have the time, but speakers both today and previously have mentioned the fact that there have to be massive infusions of capital into the CN to improve freight services in this country. Reference has been made to the present ridiculous situation where we are unable to get sufficient boxcars to move our wheat or to move our feed grains. There is a shortage of cars to move potash and a shortage of cars
January 8, 1974

to move coal. Indeed, there is a general shortage of boxcars. Surely in such a situation, instead of worrying about hotels and towers in the air, the CN should be doing something to correct this shortage of rolling stock.
We have also heard about skimping on money they have spent on the maintenance of road beds, and about how crews have been cut down to the point where there is not proper supervision, as a result of which more and more accidents are occurring than ever before. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) referred to a report which outlined some of the problem areas about which he has been warning this House for years. For example, just last week there were two serious derailments in New Brunswick. Fortunately, freight trains were involved and there was no loss of life, but there was a tremendous dollar loss. I shudder to think what might have happened had passenger trains had been passing over this roadbed. Although I have not yet seen the report on this accident, it appears that this was a case of too heavy traffic passing over the rails which the roadbed could not handle, so it gave way. Instead of spending money on hotels and towers, the CN should do something now in terms of facing up to the tremendous influx of passengers they will have to haul over the next five years as a result of the energy crisis.
Before I sit down I should like, in the limited time I have, to mention another area that has caused me a great deal of concern. This is a grey area that has been very frustrating. Every time I try to get an answer to questions we have the old game of shuffle ball, going from the Minister of Transport to the railways, then back to the minister, and so on back and forth. I am referring to the matter of pensions. This has been an ongoing grievance with the unions, rightly or wrongly-and I am not taking sides. However, what I am saying is that there must be an honest and frank appraisal of the CN pension scheme. I admit that this appraisal is now underway and we are expecting to have Judge Hall's report soon. But I certainly hope that that report will not be the end of the line. While the pension proposal that has been agreed on is a start in the right direction, it is certainly not the ultimate.
When we were discussing pensions in the committee two or three years ago, I was one of those who opposed the suggestion that pensions be made part of the bargaining package. What I have seen since then has confirmed my opinion that we made a grave mistake in suggesting that pensions be included in the bargaining package, and I should like to tell the House why I say that. When you deal with a group of employees whose ages extend from 17 to 65 you find a great difference of opinion existing among those employees. As far as the young men are concerned, they think of bills they have to pay today and tomorrow and are interested in wage increases and hours of work. They think of a pension at age 65 as something away in the future and are not interested in it. On the other hand, employees in their fifties are thinking about retirement. Therefore you find a conflict of interest, and this is apparent with the pension proposals that have been agreed upon. The younger members are quite happy with it, whereas anyone who has been employed prior to 1956 is very unhappy and feels he has been cheated. This is what happens when you bargain for a mixed group such as this.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
I do not know what the answer is. We have allowed pensions to become part of the bargaining process, and since the precedent has been established I doubt we can change the situation now. But this is one area in which the government should give direction to the CNR so that the whole pension mess will be tidied up.
In conclusion, I should like to say a few words on behalf of those ex-employees of the CN who have no one to speak for them. I refer to employees who have gone on pension and are no longer union members. These people have been continually overlooked, except of course for any representations made by individual members of the House. Now is the time when the government should tell the CNR it has a moral obligation to these people. Let us know how much is needed to bring their pensions up to a level similar to that of public service employees. If we have to find funds to do this, let us find them, but let us not have the CNR hide behind this cloak of not having the money to do it. It is for these reasons I think the amendments are good. They put into question the whole direction of CNR policy, and I hope members of the House will give them serious consideration.

speechtext: Perhaps I can be persuaded. The idea behind the amendment is that the first concern of the railroad, particularly the CNR, should be to serve Canada as a transportation system. I suggest this is a perfectly sound and useful argument. I do not know the purpose of building this tower in Toronto. It may be some kind of a prestige project so that the CNR will have the tallest building with the needle on top. It will only occupy that position of prestige until someone or some corporation somewhere decides to build a tower with a needle on top 30 feet higher. The CNR will have this sort of thing going for it, which I suppose is something, but I know a great number of people who are dependent on rail transportation, including those in industry, business and farming who will not be impressed at all by the fact that the CNR has the tallest building in Toronto. I know a great many men and women employed by the CNR who have the rather quaint idea that pensions and wages are more important than having the tallest building in the city of Toronto.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
A number of people in those categories communicate with me by telegram and by letter quite regularly regarding their concern about pensions. I received copies of two telegrams recently, one directed to the Chairman of the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Transport and Communications. This telegram is signed by Mr. H. K. Beckett, Chairman of the Biggar Railway Employees Association, in which he states:
We hereby request your presenting before transport committee suggestion for recommendation by your committee to railway arbitra-

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
tor Justice Hall that railway pension study of Commissioner Dr. Deutsch not be included in final wage and rules report of Justice Hall.
We suggest also you recommend to federal Minister of Labour, Justice Hall, and Dr. Deutsch that no action toward finalizing railway pension issue be taken prior to a hearing before your committee of the associations concerned with the railway pension issue in Canada.
The wage and rules issue under arbitration can then be concluded.
Pension study can be provided necessary time required to do a full report after House reconvenes in February 1974.
Another request I received from the same association suggested that this House continue in session until the reports of Dr. Deutsch and Justice Hall come before this House. Both of these seem to be reasonable requests. These are the types of statements being made by people throughout the country, and they do not have much to do with the building of that tower in Toronto.
Another thing which has come to my attention, and this has been mentioned by previous speakers, is the matter of rolling stock, as related to the transportation of grain and lumber, the real business of the railroad. A question which appeared in Hansard for January 7 at page 9087 is as follows:
How many railway cars designed for hauling grain have been built for Canadian National Railways in the past 12 months?
The answer to that question was none. Here we have a railway which is in the business of moving grain and, along with the CPR, is the sole method of accomplishing this movement. However, no cars have been built in the past 12 months for this purpose. The railway gives the excuse that the Canadian Wheat Board purchased 2,000 grain cars in 1972. As an excuse for doing nothing, they cite the emergency action the Canadian Wheat Board took in 1972 to provide rolling stock. Someone asked whether the railway was considering putting concrete ties or sleepers, as they are called, under the rails. The answer was no, they had no intention of modernizing the system to that extent. The company was also asked how many locomotives it leased, and the reply was that they were leasing a certain number from United States railroads. This is of real concern when we realize we have a rail transportation system under the direction of individuals who have been either unwilling or without the imagination to plan the modernization of these facilities in order to carry out the transportation task required in Canada.
If the government, on behalf of the CNR, brought a request before this House for almost any amount of money to modernize this transportation system, to purchase rolling stock or to purchase or lease locomotives, I am sure there would be no difficulty in getting approval. If the government were to bring forward proposals that would satisfy the questions that have been asked here during the last hour, and during the question period, in respect of the development of a passenger service which would rapidly move people between our large centres of population, such as Toronto, Montreal and the golden triangle, I am sure they would receive the approval of hon. members.
If the company came forward with a proposal for a well-designed system which could rapidly move feed grain into Quebec and the Maritime provinces, where it is needed, I am sure it would get approval for whatever amount of money was needed. If the company asked for money in order to improve its service between Thunder Bay and Vancouver, I am sure there would be no question

about giving approval. No one criticized the company when it proposed to double-track the line between Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie. The company has no difficulty in getting approval for this kind of improvement which is essential to the provision of a good transportation system.
Why then do we not have, through the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who in the final analysis is the responsible minister, a request to this House for the financing that is needed to provide in absolute terms a rail transport facility which can serve the needs of Canadian industry, Canadian business, Canadian farming and Canadian citizens? Why does the Minister of Transport not put such a program before the House instead of waiting around? I have asked the Minister of Transport and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board if they had assurances that the CPR and the CNR would provide the facilities to move the grain out of western Canada. Their reply was that the CNR and the CPR had given such a commitment. I do not question the ministers' sincerity in the answer they gave me, but if the CNR or the CPR have ever given that commitment, they did not live up to it. There are only 10 million bushels of wheat in Thunder Bay in facilities which have a capacity of 70 million additional bushels.
The same situation exists in Vancouver where there are only three million bushels of wheat. When you know that one boat can take a third of that amount, you realize the nature of the problem. As I said, the responsibility rests with the government. When the Canadian Transport Commission reported a couple of days ago that the safety precautions of the CNR were inadequate, what answer did they get? The Canadian National Railways said that the conclusions reached by the Canadian Transport Commission in its report last week on railway safety were based on outdated figures and did not reflect current conditions. The report is not outdated, Mr. Speaker, and it does reflect current conditions. It is the CNR which is outdated and which does not reflect current conditions. The same is true of the Minister of Transport when he brings this bill before the House.
Many Canadian citizens are getting pretty fed up with this sort of approach. I do not know who is making policy in this country with regard to railroads.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: The NDP.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is the CPR or the government. If you read the history of the CPR as it relates to the history of this country, you would find it rather difficult to untangle who was making policy, the CPR or the government. One might have reason to hope that by 1973 the government of Canada might have been able to sort out its responsibilities and to discharge them. I say that this government is not discharging its responsibility to the Canadian people in terms of railway transportation. It is a colossal failure and it stands condemned before the House for the proposals it is putting before us. Any one who sat on the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and listened to some of the answers we got when we were asking about transport could not
January 8, 1974

help but come to the conclusion that many questions were not being fully answered, that we were not receiving a full picture of the needs of Canadians.
I should like to go back to the safety report and point out that it is a disgrace to ask men to run trains under conditions which the Canadian Transport Commission says are unsafe. By what right do we, the people of Canada who own the railroad, ask men to drive trains at high speeds under conditions which are unsafe? The statement by the CNR management that the CTC's report is out of perspective, with no consideration given to the massive workload imposed on the CNR during the past decade, does not make sense. What do they mean by "massive workload during the last decade"? What do they think the CNR was created for except to carry a massive workload? It was not created as a scenic railway to run across the mountains, thus enabling people to sit in a car with some windows up on top and look at the scenery. It was created to move a massive amount of freight and passengers across the mountains. If those who are responsible for the direction of the CNR have not conveyed their need for facilities to meet the demands of the Canadian economy to the minister responsible, then they have not discharged their responsibility. If the minister responsible, having been informed of these needs, has not acted, then he is not discharging his responsibility.
This country needs somebody like Harry Truman who put up a little placard on his desk which read "the buck stops here". It is about time we had someone who had that kind of courage and that kind of attitude. This applies to the CNR and to the government in the present energy situation. However, I will not discuss the energy situation now because it is not the subject matter of our debate here. I could give you, Mr. Speaker, endless references to the requests that have come to us as members of the necessary service by both railways. These go right down to the local level. I continually receive letters and telephone calls from people in small towns in my constituency who tell me they cannot get a satisfactory express service. Most of them have given up hope of riding a train anyway, but they still hope to get some express service, either by truck or by rail. All too often they are dismayed and disappointed at the type of service they are offered. This is inexcusable.
I do not think anyone now expects a passenger train to stop at every whistle stop as it goes across Canada, but people do expect express to be delivered to the various towns by one means or another. After all, the people who live in those towns order goods which they want delivered, unless we expect to get to the point where everyone will have to get into his own individual truck or car and drive 60 or 70 miles to the nearest main shopping centre to pick up what he needs once or twice a week. That is a possibility. I grew up in the pioneer days in Saskatchewan when you did that. You just sat all winter on the farm, and twice a month hooked up a team to the sleigh and went the ten miles to town. Maybe you took in a load of grain. There, you gathered up groceries and the rest of your needs and hauled them home, then waited for another two weeks. If the concept of the government and of CN is that we should regress to those days, well, it is one way of running a country. It is not very efficient. But it is possible to slow our economy down to that pace.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
Sometimes we wonder, considering the answers we get, whether the railroads are really thinking in terms of a modern transportation system, or whether they are really thinking of how little service can be given and still get away with it. I hope that, as a result of this discussion and of the proceedings in the Transport Committee some new ideas will filter down to those responsible for running the CNR and Air Canada. Maybe some of those ideas will even reach those responsible in the government, so that instead of excuses we can have an adequate, working railway transportation system for the people of Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as an ordinary citizen living on the Prairies, even before I was of voting age, I developed certain ideas about what railways were all about, even the CNR. In those days, the railways were carrying grain from the Prairies to the ports. They were carrying goods to the Prairies, and carrying people out to the coast, as we used to say, or down east.
As a freshman member of parliament I brought some of those preconceived notions into this House with me. I thought railways, and the CNR in particular, had as their prime function railroading and that, in the course of carrying out that function, deficits might be incurred. I had heard, again before I came into this House, that the CNR was frequently required, for national, social and economic reasons, to operate lines which were not otherwise economic, in the interests of Canadian unity. That was fair enough and if, in the course of operating these lines and the main line globally, deficits were incurred then CNR could come back to this House, make its explanation, show that it had managed its affairs properly and ask for further finances in order to continue to serve the nation, carrying goods in, across and out of Canada, and carrying passengers at the same time. I understood this to be a legitimate method of operation.
Then, I began to look at some of the reports that came flying across my desk when I became a parliamentarian who still held those old fashioned notions about what railways were all about. I saw the bills that were coming in, and the reports. For example, late last year the Auditor General's report came across my desk. I was thumbing through it and I noticed that the Canadian National Railways was not one of those Crown corporations which report to parliament and have their books audited by the Auditor General. I also noted on page 187 of the 1972 report, under a heading "Loans to and Investments in Crown Corporations" there is a table which shows the comparable balances at the close of three fiscal years, 1970, 1971 and 1972, of the indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways.
In 1970, there was a total of $2,156,770,000. In 1971, it was $2,361,000,000. It had gone up about $150 million. In 1972, it was $2,590,000,000. I did not even have to make the subtraction, because I found out on page 189 that there was an increase over the previous year in the indebtedness of Canadian National Railways of $229 million, all of which was part of this $2,590,000,000.
This $229 million was itemized on page 189, and I found among other things that there was a loan to Air Canada of

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada $14 million, and then another temporary financing to Air Canada of $14,373,000, making a total of $28 million or, if you like, 10 per cent of this overdraft. So I say to myself that CNR started out being a railroad. It started to borrow money to carry on its railroading business, and then it began to go into the money business itself by lending money to another Crown corporation, Air Canada. This I found very strange. Some of my preconceived notions about what railways were all about began to crumble.
Now, I see Bill C-164. Here, there is reference to railroad property. That seems to be a legitimate requirement for funds. Then, there are funds for branch lines, again a legitimate operation, in the amount of $13 million. There is $31 million for equipment, which does not seem to be very much when you consider all the complaints we have heard about the lack of box cars to carry grain. Then, there is an item for telecommunications which is all right, Mr. Speaker. But then, we come to hotels and the CNR Tower. Here again, we find another type of activity in which the railway has become involved. First of all, it gets into the money lending business. I was talking to a colleague yesterday about this. He showed me an item for interest being paid by Air Canada, and I think it was to the CN, which amounted to something like $20 million a year. This I find most peculiar.
Corporate business in the present day has been known to diversify in order to invest its earnings. This seems to be a legitimate occupation for corporations which have profits. I would like to underline the word "earnings". There are a good number of Canadian corporations which earn more than they need for their normal activities, and so diversify. It is a form of insurance, if you like. It is insurance to help them run their other activities, but I do believe this activity is only justifiable when these are earnings from the principal operating function of a corporation such as the CNR. Let us go back and apply that principle to CN. Does it make sufficient earnings in its principal operation to justify diversifying and cross-insuring its activities? I suggest that it does not, because it seems to come back quite frequently to the Canadian parliament to seek more funds. These are not just funds for operating a railway, but funds for making pie in the sky. I find this very odd. I would rather have meals on wheels than pie in the sky made by the CNR.
I went back to my original ideas about railroads then and I do not think they were all that wrong. The Canadian National was conceived to provide transportation to those parts of Canada not served by the first railway line across the country; a most legitimate operation in the interests of Canadian unity. No one questions that. Members from this side of the House cannot bring forward measures to spend money; this must be done by the government. If the government comes forward with measures to support the legitimate activities of the railway, such as building boxcars, building grain cars and hopper cars, they will get their money quickly. I agree with the remarks made by the member who spoke just before me on this point. Why should we start building castles in the sky?
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) complained about the emphasis that was being placed on the hotel and meal business by the hon. member for

Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn). It was the hon. member for Mississauga who introduced the amendment in order to focus attention on these particular aspects. He knew that other hon. members would be speaking on other aspects of the legitimate business of the railways, and his concern was to focus attention of the activities which were at best remotely related to railroading.
I think the CN must be reminded from time to time, and this is our opportunity to do so, that they have a responsibility to this parliament and that the taxpayer is not going to continue advancing funds for non-railway activities. That is the purpose of this amendment. Surely, there are enough transportation problems for the CN to solve to keep it busy. In solving them, the CN can come to parliament and ask for financing if it should run into financing difficulties, but it must stay with its legitimate activities. We are being asked to approve $14 Vi million out of a total advance of some $225 million; about 7 per cent of the total is being requested for non-railway activities. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is time we drew the line, that we examined the activities of the CN and directed them to focus their attention on their prime activity.
On the radio this morning I heard a technical officer of the Canadian Transport Commission who was involved in the preparation of the report made on railway safety. From his comments I was surprised and dismayed to learn that Canadian railways, and CN in particular, have reduced thair track inspection standards in the past few years. There used to be a track inspection daily, and from this man's comments I understood that this inspection now takes place four times a week. It has been halved. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we complain about finding people to do jobs when there are lots of people and lots of jobs to be done. This reduction in track inspection procedures has been made, despite the fact that the track and the roadbed are being asked to carry heavier loads more frequently and at faster speeds. If this does not account for accidents, where are we to look?
Last spring I had occasion to travel home on the CNR. Just to make it real, there was an accident in northern Ontario, so our train had to be diverted to the CPR and go across 300 or 400 miles before rejoining the CN tracks. We were four or five hours late getting to the Lakehead, but I enjoyed the trip and cannot commend it highly enough to any hon. member who wishes to see what this country is all about. In the course of two or three days on the train I talked to various members of the crew and was distressed to find that the service I had been used to was seriously downgraded. I was used to seeing linen, silver and finger bowls on the dining room table. Why not?
I heard comments from American tourists who were most upset because they used to take that train back and forth across Canada for the sheer enjoyment of the good service. I am afraid they did not enjoy that particular trip. While they got the service from the people, because they were faithful servants of the railway, they did not get the service from the railway. It appeared that just before the crew set out on that trip they had been told their jobs were to be downgraded and they could like it or get off. Some of them had put in 30 years service and could not easily find other employment. I visited the chef in the kitchen and the washup crew, the whole lot, and found
January 8, 1974

that these people had been downgraded and their wages correspondingly reduced. This is no way to run a railroad, Mr. Speaker, to downgrade the whole operation.
We find the railroad that was originally set up to carry goods and people back and forth across Canada now engaged in the money lending business, the ultra high rise business and hotel business. It is a bad employer, too, which it has no right to be. A few moments ago the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) spoke about the pension problem. This is a matter which was brought to my attention soon after I became a member of this parliament. I learned that the pensions paid to railway employees in this country were absolutely disgraceful. We must ensure that this situation is remedied, Mr. Speaker. Meantime, we await with interest the report of Mr. Justice Hall. If it meets the situation of the employees, I assure you I will give it my full support.
In my naivete, also, I like to think that although there have been a good number of speeches on these amendments, and although there has been repetition about diversification, the proper functioning of the railroad, highrises and so on, these repetitions will persuade members of this House to support these amendments and have non-railways functions removed from this particular part of the bill. These repetitions may well serve the purpose. Perhaps a "once over lightly" touch is good for eggs, but not for railways. Let us hope, at any rate, that some of those who for one reason or another-or for lack of reason-would normally support this bill in its entirety, or this particular clause, will, either because some particular reference has struck home, or as reasonable beings, as railroad users, as the children of railroad users or, finally, as the representatives of retired railroad workers who receive letters complaining about the deplorable pension situation, support this particular amendment.
For these reasons I chose to stand up and make a few comments today in support of these amendments. I did this so that the CN can concentrate once again on its primary purpose, namely, that of moving goods and people across the country, since the railways should serve as a sort of unifying force, and provide, perhaps, certain associated services, but keep off the "pie in the sky" kick.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on second reading of this bill I discussed the CN tower in Toronto and suggested that that tower is being built not as a communications project, but as a PR project. Without doubt, the citizens of Toronto did not notice the tower when construction first began. Since then, newspapers in Toronto and newspapers serving other parts of Canada have been publishing photographs showing the height of the tower on such and such a day or in such and such a week. I admit that it is an imposing structure. Indeed, anyone who at the beginning opposed its construction will think it not simply imposing, but browbeating.
We know how difficult it is to resist hoopla. The construction of the CN tower in Toronto is the single largest act of PR hoopla we have seen in this country for quite some time. I do not think CN needs the tower. Actually, CP decided it did not need the tower. Let us not forget that originally the tower was supposed to be a combined
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada project. At any rate, CP felt that it did not need the tower and did not need to spend money on the tower.
I suggest, as I suggested on second reading, that CN had in mind much more than a mere tower when it decided to build that monstrosity. It wanted to swing public opinion in the Toronto region behind the metro centre project, which is the major project in the area, not the tower. The tower is simply the most evident part of the project. It serves as a lever on public opinion. Standing there, it says to the public, "Look at what CN can do for you, in building this tower. It will give you, the citizens of Toronto, the tallest tower in the world." As the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) suggested some time ago, it will be the tallest tower in the world until somebody, somewhere else, builds a taller one.
CN and CP have put a lot of pressure on the city of Toronto to develop the area south of Front Street in the way CN and CP want the area developed, which is not necessarily the way which will serve the interests of the people of Toronto or of the southern Ontario region. That is why I was afraid of the tower and opposed its construction. I felt it would be used as a PR lever; indeed, that is happening today.
In a way, the tower is symbolic of the approach of the CNR to the people of Canada and, indeed, to the members of this House. There are perhaps more shuntings in the CNR approach to parliament than you will find along CNR tracks. Members of this House today have tried to stand up and say how they feel. The railway companies of this country have been making a mockery of the original intentions behind the acts incorporating those railways. Time and time again, we have had reason to say that the interests of the people of this country have been let down. We speak of Canadian National Railways. Let us look at that name. We all know of the wag who once said that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. It is beginning to look as if the CNR is not going to be a national railway, in the sense in which that term was originally used.
It is not too often that we, in this House, stand up and compliment bodies set up by this House for their decisions. I was pleased to receive today, as I am sure other hon. members were, the report of the Railway Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission in the matter of Section 260 of the Railway Act, and in the matter of the applications by the CNR and CPR for the discontinuance of certain passenger services across Canada. Certain regions need to be served by the railways in their passenger carrying capacity. Despite this obvious need, the railways have had the gall and audacity to apply for suppression of these services. I am, therefore, pleased to read part of the decision and order of the Railway Transport Committee. It felt that there was an overriding claim on the part of the public, a claim overriding the specific and special interests of the railways. After taking into consideration the major arguments of the railways, the committee decided to turn down the application.
May I read into the record the last paragraph of the decision of the committee, as follows:
Many of the services under consideration in this Decision carry relatively few people, and, in all cases, these services operate at a level well below their capacity. This is primarily because of the marked

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
preference of the travelling public for the private automobile, and also because, in most instances, alternative means of public transport are available. But-
This is a very important "but".
-in considering the future transportation needs of the areas affected at this time, the Committee must take into account the probability of future changes in established travel patterns in Canada because of the looming energy crisis, and must see how change affects the demand for the services under review in this Decision, before considering the discontinuance of any of them. The Committee determines that these services should not be discontinued.
At long last, we are beginning to see some light at the end of the tunnel. The committee has been made painfully aware of the situation which looms before us. It calls it the "looming energy crisis". It is obvious to the committee, as indeed it should be obvious to the railways and as it is certainly obvious to most thinking people in Canada, that one of the most economical ways in money terms to transport passengers is by railway.
I know many members have travelled to other parts of the world, certainly to Europe. They have admired, and possibly even envied, the rail service offered to the people of Britain, Germany, the Netherlands and so on. If you stand in the station of Frankfurt, you will see hundreds, indeed thousands of people filing through that station, not just at rush hour, but at all times of the day. One thing that impresses most of us in this House about European railways is the scheduling. There are trains leaving for all parts at almost all times of the day. I wish to point out that it is not the presence of the passengers that causes the schedule to be so extensive, but the other way around. The fact that the schedule is extensive and does provide service attracts passengers to the railways.
One of the gambits the railways have used over the past few years in Canada to prove to this House that railway operations are not profitable has been to point out that they are not used by the Canadian public. One of the ways they have made apparent the railways are not being used has been by simply driving people away from using their services. In major ways, they have done this by cancelling trains, cancelling services, by making the simple act of getting a ticket at a railway station extremely frustrating or making the problem of getting from the railway station to one's home a difficult one, if not impossible.
I know that members of this House have had the good fortune of going to Montreal, but the misfortune of landing back at the Ottawa railway station. Just the other night I came back from Montreal along with a fair number of passengers. I had to wait outside the CN station in the cold for well over half an hour around the hour of midnight to be transported from the railway station to my home by taxi. I was not alone. A half hour after the train arrived, there were still 22 people waiting for a taxi. The reason the taxi service is so bad is there is a franchise or monopoly handed out by CNR to a particular service in this city. I must say the service is abysmal. It is almost as abysmal as the service we get at the airport here in Ottawa.
