speechtext: That's a surprise.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
I am simply trying to underline the point that in almost every way the railways are trying to chase people away from their services in order to prove that people do not want them. I doubt whether that is truly the case. I am convinced the people of Canada would be more than willing to use the railways if they provided adequate service.
A few days ago it was reported in the Globe and Mail that a study which had been made indicated that a rapid transit service could be provided from the centre of the city of Toronto to a point 20 miles east at a cost of approximately $100 million. That may sound like a staggering amount of money, but when you consider that this $100 million is for the total cost including setting up new grade levels, new approaches, building stations, refurbishing the tracks, setting up a new signals system, providing for rolling stock and so on, you discover that is not an awful lot of money. Twenty miles for $100 million is really quite cheap when you consider that expressways cost $24 million per mile. To build the same expressway facilities over the 20 mile stretch would, by simple multiplication, cost $480 million. The service provided by the expressway system may not be as fast, efficient or safe as that provided by local surface rail service.
The same article pointed out that CNR was not necessarily ready to make the right of way available for mass urban transit because it had other priorities to consider. It had priorities given to it by the statutes of this parliament and other priorities established over the years. The first priority was intercity travel. The second priority was the carrying of industrial freight, that is service to industry. Somewhere down at the bottom of the pile there was perhaps a priority, or at least a notion, which would indicate the railway had some duty toward the transportation needs of our urban populations.
If that is the case, I would like to ask where in the statutes of this country we will find the priority for real estate. I do not think we will find it. Originally, it was understood that hotels could be built to service the public travelling on the railways. However, as the railways are proud to point out, there are now very few people travelling on them. What justifies their massive interest in real estate? I suggest the very least we can do is re-inspect the priorities we have given to the railways and tell them there is indeed a very real need for the use of their tracks,

lights of way facilities, station facilities and so on by the urban travelling public in this country.
As I said a while ago, I was delighted to read the line in the transport committee report about the looming energy crisis. It should be obvious to even a beginner in high school that one of the cheapest ways to transport people over distances, long or short, is by rail, whether you calculate it in terms of kilo-calories per passenger mile or any other way.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: How do you spell that?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
M-i-l-e. There is no doubt that the most efficient use we can make of energy when it comes to transportation is through rail traffic.
Another aspect of energy conservation occurs to me. We shall need to decide very soon how the fossil fuel supply in our possession can best be used. It is obvious there are certain very inefficient ways of using it; for example, using fossil fuels, oil, let us say, to produce thermal electricity which has an end use of heating buildings is terribly inefficient. There is scarcely a thermoelectric plant which can produce electricity at an efficiency greater than 40 per cent. What we should try to do, therefore, is use fossil fuels for purposes for which other fuels are not practicable. Certain types of transportation vehicles must carry their own fuel along with them; long distance traffic could not be tied to hydroelectric wires, and neither could automobiles. Trains, on the other hand, can operate electrically with great success.
Again, if we turn to the European example we find they have managed to electrify thousands of miles of railway line. Here in Canada I doubt whether there are any lines which operate electrically. This was not always the case. We used to have electric trains, and I do not mean toy trains, either. A few years ago I was living in the City of Guelph, and at that time they were just about to extend highway 401 so it would reach Guelph. I remember saying to an old resident: Isn't it great to know that as soon as they build the 401 to Guelph you will be able to get to Toronto in an hour or an hour and ten minutes? He said: Maybe, but 50 years ago we could get there in 55 minutes. And how did he do it? By means of the electric railway which served Guelph, Barrie and other places on the line. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) says a commuter rail service is to be established between Richmond Hill and Toronto. I can, myself, remember taking a train between Quebec City and St. Anne de Beaupre. It was an electric train, a very good, fast train and I am sure it made very efficient use of the hydroelectric power produced in the area.
People have been talking lately about developing rail service in this country, particularly for rapid transit use, and there has been a tendency to talk in Flash Gordon terms about the facilities we ought to install. The Prime Minister of Ontario has proposed an elevated linear-motored railway of European design for Toronto. The design has not really been tested yet, so there is a proposal to test it at the CN Exhibition within a year or so. All kinds of machines are tested on exhibition grounds. Ferris wheels and roller coasters are tested there and they work
Canadian National Railways
very well, but I doubt that the context of an exhibition will give us any real opportunity to test the workability of this futuristic and questionable design. On the other hand, there is much experience from years past of the efficient use of light rail traffic, and we do not need to go very far to re-establish the use of this kind of traffic along rights of way which serve urban populations.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June, 1974, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and motions Nos. 1 and 2 (Mr. Blenkarn).

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the key word in this debate is surely the word "priorities". The question is not whether the railroad should be erecting and maintaining hotels; it is not whether the railroad should be erecting and operating a communications tower. The question is this: what does the railroad value most? What does it regard as its chief social obligation? It is clear from the debate which has taken place that hon. members across this country from one coast to another, the representatives of the people, are not convinced that

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
this national railway is putting people first. It is clear that service to the people does not enjoy the priority we expect it to be given. Instead, we find the thinking of the executives of the CN is dominated by what might be called a "monumentality"; it is striving to erect a monument to the system itself rather than using available resources to develop the services which our society urgently needs.
As one thinks of what the spokesmen for the railway had to say when defending the construction project one is reminded of the movie, starring Charlie Chaplin a generation ago, called "The Great Dictator". Chaplin and Jack Oakie played the parts of Hitler and Mussolini and in one scene they were seated in two adjacent barber chairs. First one jacked up his chair, and then the other, until finally each of them was hitting the ceiling. We get the impression that executives are motivated by a desire to erect a building higher than those possessed by their rivals. What we are criticizing is not the construction of a hotel or a communications tower but, rather, projects which take first claim on the resources of the railway company at a time when the primary need is the service of the people, particularly the improvement and introduction of rapid transport facilities in major urban areas such as Metropolitan Toronto.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
It is more in the interest of the ordinary person in Toronto that the rights-of-way entering into the heart of this massive metropolitan area be used for rapid public transit than resources be committed to some tourist attraction. The proposed tower may become an interesting construction which many visitors to the city will enjoy seeing; they may derive a certain pleasure from eating pie in the sky in a revolving restaurant a thousand feet above ground, but the real need of the working people is for efficient, rapid transit within their financial capacity.
Within the Toronto area there is mile after mile of line which could be used in this fashion. Indeed, a report of the CNR recently issued indicated it was possible to adapt a right-of-way for rapid transit purposes, connecting Toronto Union Station and Pickering, a distance of 20 miles, at a total cost of only $100 million. This averages out at $5 million per mile, in contrast to the $24 million per mile proposed for the Scarborough expressway. If this project is feasible, and according to the research study made by the CNR it is, surely it is incumbent upon all authorities concerned, including the railroads, the federal government and the local authorities, to give such construction priority. That is the purpose of this debate. It is not that we are against anything as much as that we want a reallocation of values. We want a renewal of the policy that puts people first, of the policy that asks what it is that people in this area require most.
What can be said about the needs of the people of metro Toronto can also be said of the needs of people in communities right across this land. One of the things that disturbs me is the lack of initiative being shown by the government in regard to meeting the needs of people in the various urban centres of Canada. For years now the

CNR has financed the deficits that have been incurred by the commuter service into the city of Montreal. For example, in 1970 the CNR had to pick up a deficit of $2.1 million. In 1971, the deficit was $2.2 million and in 1972 it was $2.4 million.
I do not criticize the CNR for picking up these deficits in operating Montreal commuter trains; I think the commuter service into Montreal is a fine one that meets the needs of a vast number of people. If the CNR were picking up the deficits of a commuter service into Toronto, then I expect a lot of people would object. From all corners of the country as well as from all corners of this House, we would hear words of protest. But here is something being done to meet the needs of people living in a major metropolitan centre of Canada, and we would like to see the same kind of initiative being taken both by the company and the government to meet the needs of vast numbers of people in other centres who are trying to make their way to work and home again day by day.
Fortunately, the federal government is at last shaking itself out of its lethargy on this issue. We recently had an announcement regarding partial federal financing of a commuter train service from Richmond Hill to Toronto. However, I note that the maintenance costs of that service will be have to be borne by the Ontario government, including all deficits. In this regard we would like, first of all, to acknowledge the initiative that the federal government has shown, but we would go on to ask, does the government have to stop there? Although it may not be too little, too late, it is certainly too little in light of the needs of today's society.
What bothers me is that day after day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), when asked serious and practical questions by members of parliament, stands up and defends his lethargy by saying that he has no real influence over the CNR. I point out that the CNR is totally owned by the people of Canada, and the minister, as spokesman for the people of Canada, surely has a responsibility to get the CNR to take action. Expressways and city streets are clogged with cars and trucks day after day and can rightly be described as the largest parking lots in this country. On the other hand, vast railroad rights-of-way are lying empty. Thus, we wonder at the lack of initiative on the part of this so-called Minister of Transport. We would say to him that, good as this gesture of assistance to metro Toronto is in terms of the Richmond Hill-Toronto commuter service, it is not enough for the people of the area. Certainly, it is not enough when we add up the needs of communities in every province in this country.
I would couple with this the need for the railroad itself to begin again to give priority to the provision of passenger service. One of the things that impressed me from reading the opinions of railroad executives was the way in which they seemed to be rather unhappy about having to carry passengers at all, and on those occasions when I have travelled by train I have been impressed by how fitting their opinions have turned out to be. If the railways say they simply want to carry freight, they sometimes give me the impression they are treating people like freight. There was a time when riding on a train was a reasonably pleasurable experience. Now, you cannot even get a decent
January 8, 1974

meal on a train or find a railway journey that is enjoyable. In this time of crisis we would submit to the leaders of the government and the management of the railroad companies that it is absolutely imperative to begin to give priority to railroad passenger service once again.
I say that for three reasons. First of all, there is a pollution crisis in our cities through over-use of gasoline powered motors. For example, in the United States the environmental protection agency has ordered that all cities in the U.S. reduce hydrocarbon emissions by 93 per cent by the year 1977. Pollution has reached a critical stage and we must liberate ourselves from our dependency upon gasoline powered motors.
My second reason is congestion. In metropolitan Toronto alone there is a concentration of 850,000 motor vehicles, about one for every 2.3 persons in the urban area. This degree of congestion is strangling metro, as it is strangling every urban community in North America.
My third reason is allocation. We have been presented with a bill that calls for the appointment of an energy allocation board. This legislation purports to set up an agency to allocate energy according to need. I should like to use this word "allocation" in order to focus the attention of the House upon the need to allocate transportation services to the end that we will have adequate railroad services which will liberate us from our dependency upon motorcars, upon expressways, upon the kind of transportation facilities that today are polluting our cities, congesting them and making us overly dependent upon oil resources.
Therefore, we urge the CNR and all of the railroad companies in the land, along with the government, which surely has some responsibility here, to give priority to people in this country, and to see to it that the railroads offer them the opportunity to do something serious and creative in the urban communities in this land. These communities are presently facing a transit crisis, but these communities can find a solution to this crisis if railroad rights-of-way are used to their maximum potential. Therefore, instead of giving priority to the development of new tourist attractions which the people may or may not need, we wish the CNR would give priority to working out with the provincial and local authorities, with the encouragement and support of the federal government, ways by which existing railway tracks and rights-of-way can be utilized for rapid public commuter transportation which would free our great cities which are now in danger of strangling to death.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is one thing about this debate that is more notable than any other, and that is the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand).

speechtext: His parliamentary secretary is here.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA

speechtext:
We have both expressed our opinion, Mr. Speaker, so we will let the matter stand there.
We are talking about transportation and amendments to this bill. During the discussion of this bill in the committee and in the House, a wide range of policy needs have been expressed by members interested in the subject of transportation in general, with air and rail transportation being the principal subjects. There has been a very distinct attack on the transportation system in Canada by those who have studied the system, by those who have used the system and by those who have written about it.
Let us look at the press of December 24, where we find a report that the Deputy Minister of Transportation has indicated that governments will have to decide how to make the most efficient use of fuel, money and the facilities of transportation. Members of this House have stated time and time again that one of the building blocks, perhaps even the cornerstone of our economy as we move from sea to sea, is the transportation facilities with which we are provided. Inasmuch as the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada are government owned in their entirety, it becomes the responsibility of government to see that these services are rendered in the interests of the public.

speechtext:
Certainly, we can find fault with individuals in the administrative staff of Air Canada and individuals in the administrative and operating staffs of the railroad. We can cite instances where individuals have not served the public as public servants should, but the whole blame in respect of poor administration can be clearly and squarely laid on the Minister of Transport and the government of which he is a member. That burden of responsibility has been shrugged off with a degree of irony and sarcasm. We have seen reports submitted to the minister in respect of the needs of this nation, and I suggest the responsibility rests with the minister, yet he has not spoken, nor has anyone else on the government side, in a responsible way about these needs.
Let us take as an example the meeting which took place in Nova Scotia more than a year ago. A report in respect of this meeting appeared in the Chronicle-Herald of January 7, as follows:
More than a year ago, a transportation "crisis" seminar was held in Wolfville, following which the sponsor, the Annapolis Valley Affiliated Boards of Trade .. . pressed Ottawa and the provincial governments for a better deal in transportation. High on the list of recommendations was boosted subsidy rates to assist Atlantic businessmen.
That sparked a meeting between the Council of Maritime Premiers and Transport Minister Jean Marchand last April, at which time it was proposed that subsidies on westbound goods would be boosted.

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
This meeting was in April, and the date of commitment was January 1, we presume of 1974 although the article does not say so. The article continues:
Atlantic-area residents, weary of decades of pleading for more help and less hinderance from Ottawa in the East's bid for a fair and just transportation deal, can only hope that the federal government will be just as slow to approve freight rate increases as it has been to grant better subsidies.
The effect of any subsidy is apparently again to be wiped out, because we find that the railroads are now asking for a substantial increase in rates, as high as 33 lA per cent in some parts of Canada. We find also that there is considerable concern about safety on the railroads. In 1959, there were 40 trains which went off the tracks. In 1969, the total had climbed to 69, and in 1972 it jumped to 132. This, then, became the subject of a board of inquiry under the Canadian Transportation Commission. Again, I submit that this is one aspect of the matters with which this bill deals. It deals with money to be spent for facilities in transportation, and safety is a very vital area in which money should be spent. The report of that commission suggested a slowdown for trains using existing tracks. I ask what this will do to an industry which is already short of cars? What will this do to a country which is pleading for a better transportation system, more efficient and faster movement of goods across the country?
The policies of this government, as embodied in the 1967 act, have permitted a decline in the safety of railways to the point where accidents have increased from 40 in 1959 to 132 in 1972. The government has sat idlely by while the railroads have reduced their maintenance staffs by roughly 80 per cent from what they were 40 or 50 years ago when trains were moving slower and hauling smaller loads. There is reference in this report to the inspection of the tracks. This inspection was carried out on a daily basis as the crews went back and forth on their little cars. The tracks were inspected superficially by eye, and the crews stopped for a closer inspection where necessary, using the appropriate tools. Today, it may be weeks before a maintenance crew ever sees a piece of track. Of course, there has to be an inspection survey, but what has been the result of the cut in the work force?
Just a matter of weeks ago, I was talking with a friend of mine who happens to be a reasonably senior engineer on one of our rail lines. He told me that if he knew any other way to make a living he would get out of his engine. He said that the safety precautions on the railway were so much poorer than when he started some 20 years ago it was shocking. He said the only reason he did not get out of the service was that he had so much invested in his pension, such as it is, he could not afford to quit. After many years of service his opinion was that the application of safety measures had deteriorated.
Under this government, and under the 1967 act as administered by the CTC, we find that the application of safety measures has deteriorated in a frightful way, detrimental to the best interests of Canada. There is only one group of people responsible for that situation. The president of the CNR is not entirely responsible: it is the policy under which the government has allowed the CNR to operate; and it is the ministers, not just the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) but all the ministers in the shuttle service that has been provided by the Prime Minis-

ter (Mr. Trudeau) and by the Minister of Transport. That shuttle service has included several ministers, and they are all jointly responsible for this decline. It is detrimental to the safety and the economics of this nation. Let us put the blame squarely where it belongs-on the shoulders of the government, the Minister of Transport and the Prime Minister.
All these little side efforts of the CNR give me great concern. I am concerned because the tower that is now being built in Toronto was initially intended to be a joint project: it was to be a CP-CN structure. We already have co-operation and joint ownership of a communications system in this country with CN-CP stockholders. Why did the CPR not want to participate in investment in the tower? Why did they accept other real estate opportunities rather than invest their money in the tower? One can only guess that the answers were not forthcoming when this bill was investigated in the committee. I think one must assume, from the lack of information, that we have put ourselves in a position of commitment with respect to the tower, that it was not to be as profitable as was suggested by some and that CPR found it more advantageous to invest money elsewhere or accept other land development opportunities. This is what one would normally assume. If that is not the case, then let us have an answer. Why did they get out? The answer was not forthcoming.
We have had car shortages in the lumber industry, the grain industry and in agriculture in general. We have had difficulties in the transportation of fertilizer, to name but a few products that have had a squeeze. This squeeze did not come upon us without statistical evidence being relayed to the government to indicate that it was about to happen. Wc have had an increase in tonnage handled and cars loaded in the rail structure of the country over the years, and at the time that increase in loading has been taking place there has been a decline in the number of cars available for the railroads to carry the increased load.
The statistical evidence is available in the various documents presented to the committee, and in other locations as well. Why would any government allow a decline in the carrying capacity to take place on an annual basis when the load requirement was increasing on an annual basis? It is all right to say that the wheat and lumber movements were unusual, but the railroad has to base its operation on the long-term average and the anticipated increases which accrue in the business of this nation. An intelligent government would have ensured that the CNR was following the direction of the statistics and was prepared to accept the extra burden of transportation which inevitably was to come upon it. It is not unusual for transportation or any other industry to run on a cyclical basis, and I do not blame management; I blame the government for the fact that this cycle could not be met.

speechtext:
The ordinary course of events would have led the government in a different direction had it taken the care to take a look at things. One of the things about the system under which we operate is that the National Transportation Act of 1967 was supposed to set us up in a
January 8, 1974

competitive business so far as transportation is concerned.
I am quite prepared to accept the fact, as has been pointed out in particular by members on the extreme left of this side of the House, that there are some debt problems so far as CNR is concerned. But when we make this allegation I wonder whether we should not at the same time take a look at the bonded indebtedness of the competitor. If the CNR is not competitive with the CPR, the government should correct that situation. That is the first thing. Second, the government should say to the management of CNR, "Moneywise you are competitive. Now get to the business of hauling freight, and make it competitive."
The CPR has no competition. There is no point in blaming the CPR for what is happening. It is this government's administration of an enterprise which makes it unnecessary for that structure to be competitive and to seek out new business. This is the burden which has been loaded on CNR management. If it is unequitable and unjust, then the government, as the owner, should put them in a competitive position and say to them, "Gentlemen, get out and do the business as any businessman would." The government cannot compete in the free enterprise world if it cannot make a profit. Let us set up a financial structure in the CNR so that it is competitive with private enterprise. At the moment the structure is such that any user of the rails is paying the maximum tariff that his commodity will bear, and in some instances more than it can bear so that he is forced to disappear from the business world. If you look at the rates in eastern Canada, for instance, in the movement of grain you will find that grain is being moved on ton-mile rates which vary by 300 per cent.
I am not referring to western grain, but there are areas of surplus grain in this country. It is not competitive for the producer or for the railways, and it is just convenient for the railways to extract from that commodity, in certain locations in Canada, three times as much tariff as it is extracting in other areas. That is the type of management which the government has tolerated in the industry which it owns.
We find ourselves in an energy crisis, and without a policy in transportation which would show any awareness of energy savings that can be made. There has been no policy statement to indicate that transportation can be used in such a fashion as to conserve energy and, as the previous speaker said, to extend our petroleum reserves for as long a period as possible. There has been no such policy from the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), the Prime Minister or anybody else. But there is a policy to build a tower, to refurnish hotels-and now we are asked to approve the unrelated expenditure of money under a transportation bill.
This morning I had a call from a dealer in grain in eastern Canada. On December 10 or 11 the subject of grain was raised in the committee when it was discussing the financing of the CNR. We were assured in the committee that the problem would be resolved. A meeting was held in the maritime provinces on December 17, if my memory serves me correctly. The Wheat Board representatives, the feed grain board representatives, feed purchasers and railroad officials-all the people interested in the transportation, provision and consumption of grain were there. But
Canadian National Railways
the call I received this morning told me that there are cars of grain, for which orders have been accepted, which have not moved since December 21. I am told that the grain available will be delivered irrespective of grade, and that the customers must accept the substitution which the Wheat Board wishes to impose.
If our transportation system is to be planned as the Wheat Board plans it for this kind of mix-up, then it is high time the government took a hand and found out what policy is necessary, because friends of mine are moving grain back and forth, trading it back and forth within their own mills so that those mills can continue to operate.
Even after the promise made by various cabinet ministers that this problem would be corrected forthwith, and even after the meeting was held in Moncton and assurances were given that the problem would be corrected, the problem is still acute in some areas. True, there has been an improvement. I can say this to the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, and to the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board; but there is still much to be desired when a car of grain has been on order since December 21 and it has not yet rolled away from the elevator. That is a long while for a chicken to wait for feed. For once I can agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave). It is high time we had a definite government policy on transportation.

Mr. Speaker, as I look around this chamber it is worth noting that the only members of the cabinet here to listen to this debate on the CNR financing bill are the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) and the Minister of State (Mr. Haidasz), who is responsible for multicultural affairs. I appreciate that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) might not want to show their faces around here when this kind of legislation is being debated. I suppose I should not speak ill of the two ministers who are here: there is no doubt in my mind that the Minister of State knows at least as much about transport as the Minister of Transport.
My reason for speaking on these amendments is my belief that before the Canadian taxpayer is asked by the government to support CN hotels and grandiose projects such as the CN tower, he should at least be entitled to decent transportation provided by the CNR. My party's position on this is quite distinct from the position of the other two parties. The Liberals argue that whatever the management of CN wants to do is all right with them, and the NDP complains that CN has so badly served Canadians in providing such poor rail service that it should be given even more public money to waste on hotels that run into the red and on obscene monstrosities such as the CN tower. Our position is that until CN can do a decent job as a railway, its management should not be allowed to indulge in empire building in unrelated areas.

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
I regret that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) is not in the chamber. I could not help but feel a sense of wonder and awe as I followed his agile mind at work last night. He complained about the CN board of directors, he complained about the problems of the western farmer in getting proper service from the CN, and he complained that the railway does not meet the transportation needs of the people. But what was his answer to the problem of inept public management of this company? It was that the government should take over CP rail as well.

speechtext:
wonder whether I might be permitted to share with the hon. member who said "hear, hear", and with my other socialist friends, a story I heard recently that illustrates the sort of logic that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre uses when he says that the answer to the problem of too much socialism is more socialism. The constituency I have the honour to represent is largely rural. It contains some of the finest agricultural land in Canada. The eastern part of it, in Dufferin county, has considerable potato production.
The story is told about a couple of city slickers who decided that they would come up and make a quick dollar from the potato farmers in Melancthon township. The two were a father and son team from Toronto by the name of David and Stephen. They got in their truck and drove from farm to farm, buying up large bags of potatoes at $5 a bag until their truck was full. From there they drove into Shelburne, one of the local small towns, parked on the street and sold their potatoes for $5 a bag to the town's residents. Before long all the potatoes were sold, and they went home for the night. The next day they drove up again to Dufferin county and proceeded to buy potatoes at $5 for a big bag until their truck was once more full. Then they drove into Orangeville, where they parked on the side of the road and proceeded to sell their potatoes for $5 a bag to the local residents. By the end of the day all the sacks had been sold. After they had totalled up their earnings for the day, Stephen turned to David and said, "You know, dad, we haven't been making too much money on this deal." To which David replied, "You're right. I've been thinking about what we have to do about that. I've decided it's time we got ourselves a bigger truck." That is an example of the sort of logic employed by my socialist friends who claim that when the government has botched things up the only solution is to give the government more power.
I come from a constituency that has been ill served by the government and by the two railways. The private company would rather haul garbage than people to my area, destroying prime farmland in the process. Both it and the CNR have discontinued passenger service to my area, so that today not one passenger train passes through it. The effect of the discontinuance has been damaging to the development of the small towns which depend upon decent transportation for their survival. Many of our senior citizens have been trapped, unable to visit family and friends outside their home towns.

Each member of parliament from the area has had numerous complaints about the failure of both companies to keep their fences up and the weeds in check. But the answer of the railways is to strip back the number of section crews and the equipment those hardworking men need to do a proper job. In the meantime roadbeds are allowed to deteriorate to the point where trains have to be run upon them at reduced speed for safety. We have already reached the point where passenger service could not be restored without rebuilding vast stretches of roadbed in the area. And what is the answer of the government? It is to ask the Canadian people to spend their tax money subsidizing CN management's edifice complex while the area goes begging for decent treatment from the railways.
Repeatedly the people of my area have asked for help from the federal government, and repeatedly they have been refused. Even when the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, which at the time had a Liberal chairman, a Liberal co-chairman and a Liberal majority, unanimously recommended in June, 1972, that service be restored, the government simply refused to act. When he was asked in this House what action he was going to take on the matter, the Minister of Transport, who confused the problem of the area with that of commuters trying to get to their jobs in Toronto, equivocated, stalled and talked of negotiations with the government of Ontario, or of local participation in the formulation of policy as requested by the municipalities.
He then simply conducted a local Gallup poll that completely bypassed municipal governments. And after claiming in the House yesterday, "I have received a report and it has been communicated to all interested parties", he disclosed that he suppressed the report for over a month, maybe because he does not feel that the local members of parliament, the affected municipalities, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and the people of the area involved are interested parties.
Yet with this sort of record the government asks for the support of this House to give even more money to the CNR for projects that have nothing to do with the company's primary function, namely, running a railroad in an efficient manner. Mr. Speaker, the minister did not want to be made Minister of Transport. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave him his present portfolio after he had dropped the ball so badly as minister responsible for DREE and as campaign manager for the Liberal Party in Quebec that he had become an embarrassment to the government. If the minister still does not want this department, or if he is simply incompetent, then surely the people of southwestern Ontario should not be burdened with him. The Prime Minister should relieve him of his present responsibility and appoint him to the Senate where he can join the host of Liberal bagmen and campaign officials who are already working on the next election campaign at public expense. At least if he were in the Senate he could do no more damage to the people of my area.
The people of southwestern Ontario are a hardworking, industrious and independent group. They do not ask the government for hand-outs but they do believe that they
January 8, 1974

are entitled to the same sort of treatment from the government and the CNR as they would receive if they came from the Minister of Transport's riding. And they do not believe that their tax money should be going to subsidize hotels and CN towers until they have received the kind of service they deserve right now from the government and the CNR.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the House deals primarily with priorities in the expenditure of money by Canadian National Railways. The amendment states that money should not be appropriated for the building of CN towers and hotels.
Keeping in mind that the amendment relates to priorities and spending, I should like to say a few words about the participation of CN in the GO commuter service. I was delighted to learn yesterday that the government had agreed to give $13 million toward the operation of this service between Toronto and Richmond Hill. The province of Ontario has already agreed to operate a GO service between Toronto and Georgetown, the latter being 20 miles from the city which I have the honour to represent, namely, Guelph. The city of Guelph has a population of some 66,000 people. The present plan is to terminate the GO service at Georgetown and take the people by bus the 20 miles from Guelph to Georgetown. I do not think it is a proper priority for the CNR to stop the GO train at Georgetown and ask people from Guelph to take the bus for those 20 miles and then transfer to the GO train to Toronto.
1 appeal to the CNR to extend this GO service to the city of Guelph for the following reasons: first, the track is already there and, second, the equipment will be provided; the staff will be provided and the general overhead will be more or less the same. There is a place in Guelph where the GO train could stay overnight. The trains are heated electrically, so that is no problem. They could start and finish at the city of Guelph as easily as they can at Georgetown. When they think of priorities, I would hope the CNR, along with the province of Ontario, would consider extending the GO train service those extra few miles to the city of Guelph. There is presently a CN train which leaves Guelph early in the morning and comes back at night, but I understand this train is to be taken off. I am pleased that the government has seen fit for the first time to give money to the GO commuter service in Ontario. This proves that the private member's bill which I introduced last July, an act to amend the Railway Act, which simply recommended that commuter trains should be treated like any other service for the payment of subsidies on losses, has had some effect.
Speaking of priorities, Mr. Speaker, the CN line from Toronto to Stratford and on to Sarnia needs greater attention. Between Christmas and the New Year that train came into the city of Guelph; it was composed of three rail-liners which are three self-propelled cars hooked together. There was standing room only on these three cars and about 75 people were waiting to board them at Guelph. Surely the management of CNR could see the need for proper equipment at peak times such as this. It is
Canadian National Railways
hard for people to understand why the proper equipment is not available.
If we are to help in the environmental problem and to play our part in fighting the energy crisis, surely the railways must realize that they have an important part to play as well. They must realize that the main lines of the railways are here to stay and must be maintained and kept in good condition both as to track and general equipment. This must be a top priority. But I would say, Mr. Speaker, that as far as the CN is concerned the matter of priority leaves much to be desired.
I close by saying what I said at the beginning. I feel that the GO commuter train service for all provinces in Canada should be subsidized for losses. I am happy to know that the government has recognized this need and has seen fit to help the Ontario line. I hope that assistance will be available for other GO line services in other large urban areas of Canada. In the particular case in which I am primarily interested, I hope the GO train will go the full distance and will give the people of Guelph the service to which a city with a population of 65,000 is entitled.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the amendments to Bill C-164, I wish to state that I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) with regard to reducing expenditures by CNR and Air Canada. I submit that no money should be paid to Air Canada until MOT has conducted an investigation into complaints registered by employees, members of parliament and the general public and a report has been made to parliament.
If one compares Air Canada with other airlines one will see the the operations of Air Canada leave much to be desired. Air Canada's virtual monopoly of Canadian air travel creates difficulty in measuring its productivity. There are no available Canadian companies of comparable size. Delta offers an example of an airline of comparable size in the competitive U.S. market. The comparison is one of a monopolistic public airline versus a private airline in a highly competitive market.
Let us compare assets. Air Canada possessed more total assets than Delta. Air Canada had assets totalling $834,262,000, while Delta had assets totalling $780,706,000. In spite of greater assets, Air Canada had less operating revenues. Delta had operating revenues valuing $757,569,-
9164

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
000; Air Canada's operating revenues totalled $583,272,000. Therefore, while Air Canada had $54,556,000 greater assets than Delta, it had $174,307,000 less in operating revenues. It is interesting to note that the advantage of Air Canada in total assets is not to be found in the number of aircraft. Air Canada possessed 102 aircraft while Delta possessed 138. More specifically, Delta had 22,105,725 available seat-miles while Air Canada had only 12,169,049.
If one compares expenses one will see that Air Canada incurred fewer operating expenses than Delta. Delta's expenses totalled $682,117,000, while Air Canada's totalled $537,770,000. Although Delta's over-all expenses were higher, Air Canada spent $2,975,000 more on general and administrative expenses and $8,448,000 more on promotion and sales. In the area of passenger service Delta spent $1,513,000 more than Air Canada. Therefore, while Air Canada spent more on administration, promotion and sales, it spent less on passenger service.
A comparison of productivity indicates that Air Canada experienced a yield of 6.02 cents revenue per passenger-mile while Delta managed a yield of 6.50 cents. Therefore, Delta produced 8 per cent more in revenue per passenger-mile. This was accomplished in spite of a 17 per cent lower passenger load factor. Delta was also more efficient in cargo. Delta experienced expenses of 22.20 cents per available ton-mile while Air Canada experienced 24.28 cents. An historical survey of these operating expenses reveals that Delta has held them at a more stable rate. Air Canada fluctuated from 28 cents in 1963 to 22 cents in 1971.
Also speaking against the record of Air Canada is the brief submitted to members of parliament by the Canadian Air Line Employees Association. This brief, in criticizing Air Canada operations, deals first with procedures. It says:
Airline procedures sometimes seem to disregard reality entire. For example:
(1)	It is unrealistic to believe that employees may use the public address system regularly to summon supervisors or other staff members while at the same time they refuse public requests for a page on the grounds that they are not permitted to page. The customer does not know that it is a supervisor being paged at the same time that his request is refused-and he probably would not care. The purpose of the policy is eminently reasonable-i.e. the inaccessibility of the PA due to public pages; the method used to effect some control is completely irrational.
(2)	Qualified ticket agents were permitted to handle only domestic tickets in some offices until an indefinite point in the far distant future when the supervisor decided to designate them "international agents''.
Also, the union claims that initiation of automated check-in procedures at some airports had made it impracticable to attempt to offer some services which were available under manual procedures. For example, a seat request might be accommodated under a manual procedure; the request would not normally be considered under one-stop check-in procedures. Unfortunately, none of the company manuals or local bulletins have reflected the inability of an airport to consider such requests. The CALEA brief also comments on facilities. Working conditions have been so bad at times that the staff have threatened to leave the premises. Recently, the following incidents, symptomatic of problems in offices across the system, have occurred:

first, the heat in a ticket office became so intense that the manager refused to work there and a customer fainted; second, the temperature in an airport lobby reached 34 degrees. The management personnel on duty refused to take any corrective action until the union threatened to withdraw the staff and a senior union officer was called to the scene.
Then third, staff have had to complain long and bitterly about the failure of cleaning firms to maintain the premises in a clean manner. Fourth, safety hazards, such as loose wires on the floor, have been permitted to continue in the face of formal protests. In one instance an employee was injured so seriously that he was off work for approximately two months before corrective action was effected. Fifth, a cashier in one busy airport has a cubicle which is completely open in the rear to a well-frequented corridor. Although this fact is easily discernible, management do not feel there is any cause for alarm.
Then sixth, a cash register was provided for a major ticket counter which was too small to handle the volume of cash over more than two to three hours. The cashier then had a choice-leave the cash drawer open with money bulging out, or stop serving the customers briefly while the money was transferred to a safe. Seventh, employee rest facilities are dismal for the most part. Washrooms tend to be tiny, dull and sometimes dirty. Lunchrooms tend to be poorly furnished. In some bases, even the larger ones, there is not even a couch available in case an employee becomes ill and needs to lie down. The recent renovations at the Calgary airport have virtually created a firetrap for Air Canada counter employees.
It is a temptation to continue to recite further examples of poor facilities. The inadequacies cover a wide range of possibilities, as the examples indicate. Under "staffing" in the CALEA presentation it is stated that demands for overtime coverage and greater productivity have increased. The amount of overtime required, particularly for IAM and CALEA personnel, is known to have exceeded the federal maximum hours permitted, yet to our knowledge no report has been sent to the minister as required by law. Because of these increased demands, staff in some areas are suffering from some degree of mental, neural and/or emotional stress.
Air Canada has no known method for staffing their ticket offices. Maximum staff is limited by the facilities themselves. Shifts and meal/rest periods are scheduled in such a way that the staff on duty is greatest during the periods of greatest demand, normally during the noon hour. There are no published standards or statistics available to provide such information as maximum desired waiting period per customer, actual waiting period per customer per hour over extended periods in the past, or anticipated increase in customer demand.
The CALEA brief also refers to standards of Air Canada. Air Canada establishes levels of service which may vary between locations, for example offices such as airport, reservations or ticket offices, or between bases such as geographic areas, usually an urban area such as Montreal. Budget requests for the staff required to provide the level of service deemed acceptable in each location are subject to approval from more senior levels of manage-
January 8, 1974

ment. It is not unusual for these requests to be refused and an arbitrary cut in staff ordered.
With regard to automation there is great frustration among Air Canada employees. This is particularly evident in the case of one-stop check-in at airport locations. The airline cannot emphasize too strongly the need for accurate passenger counts, both because of the economic need to fill its aircraft and the safety aspect which demands an exact computation of the weight and balance of an aircraft. The anticipated computer load figures become increasingly inaccurate as each day progresses because no attempt is made to update passenger records to release space on later flights when it is no longer required.
The actual computer check-in totals may be seriously in error due to human error by the agents who operate it, customers who travel on other flights after they have been checked in, customers who are "lobby noshos" and miss their flight, computer malfunctions, and so on. The airline has recognized these problems and reinstated a manual procedure to verify the computerized check-in. Agents now verify the passenger count on board the aircraft before a flight is closed off. In the event of a computer malfunction, the agent may be forced to simply fill the aircraft and release it as he has no access to any information of the flight status, seat selection or passenger reservations. On a multi-destination flight this could affect several stations.
Also, under the heading of "employee morale" the brief states that with regard to relations, when one sees the age-old methods appear again in negotiations and grievances it is useless to claim to be more receptive when, in fact, management acts in as authoritarian a manner as ever. How senseless it is to claim to be concerned with correct procedures and administration of contract terms while at the same time members of management are imposing new and arbitrary interpretations which are bitterly contested by both the employees and the union. Women still have great difficulty in obtaining promotion. Frequently the person promoted is still the person who adhered to the party line or drank beer with the right people.
The company claims to be sincerely concerned for the welfare of its employees. Obvious safety hazards are permitted to continue. An example is the Air Canada facilities at Calgary airport. If an employee is overpaid, he is treated as if he had intentionally appropriated the money and all pay is withheld until the debt is discharged; yet if an employee is underpaid he may spend months attempting to recover his salary. One employee was underpaid in excess of $400 at the beginning of September, yet to date he has not received any satisfaction nor even a hope of satisfaction from the company.
Management ineptitude is sometimes so obvious that it cannot be overlooked. To quote one example, computerized check-in for one-stop check-in was installed in one location at a great deal of expense. When the installation was completed it was discovered that the counters were of the wrong height. An agent could neither sit nor stand in comfort on these counters. Needless to say, productivity suffered considerably.
Poor supervision is a predictable result when the company does little or nothing to select its most promising
Canadian National Railways
people and expose them to training and development courses in such pertinent areas as human and labour relations. These areas reflect problems similar to those experienced by CALEA members, although we do not have specific statistics to quote.
Also, the CALEA document mentions standards. They claim they have no information on the manner in which the standards are established for the various functions such as aircraft services, baggage, commissary, etc. The Winnipeg office also comes in for a great deal of criticism. Winnipeg is presently the site of Air Canada's financial operations. Much concern has been expressed in newspapers and by members of parliament regarding a rumoured move of the accounting computer from Winnipeg to Montreal. Naturally, Air Canada has denied any intention of moving their present Winnipeg accounting operations to Montreal. From past experience, including the manner in which Air Canada moved its operations from Winnipeg to Montreal, can one really accept the denials proferred by Air Canada? It should be noted that the first move is to take the computers from Winnipeg to Montreal and that this process is already under way. Can the rest of the accounting operation be far behind?
Another recent event in the finance branch of Air Canada was the transfer to Chicago or Toronto of the function of making up AC-CN credit cards. As well, the CALEA document comments on labour relations. For years Air Canada has attempted to suppress organized labour, and today their attitude is unchanged: it remains as it was before reorganization. In CALEA's opinion, Air Canada does not place enough emphasis on labour relations. This opinion is more than substantiated by the series of labour difficulties experienced by Air Canada in the past five years, with all the unions involves in strikes, partial strikes and slowdowns. The unions that deal with Air Canada also deal with Pacific Western Airlines. It is interesting to note that Pacific Western Airlines has been able over the past few months to conclude agreements with most of its unions in record time. One can only conclude that if Air Canada were to show an enlightened attitude toward organized labour, all parties concerned would benefit.
To summarize the CALEA brief, an attempt is made throughout to place emphasis on people-Air Canada's customers and employees. The tragic truth is that Air Canada does not recognize people as being all that important. They seem to place dollars above all else. It is so simple. If Air Canada became people-oriented, improvements could easily be achieved in employee morale, customer service, labour relations and profitability. Air Canada employees who are CALEA members are conscientious employees. However, they are disturbed and concerned about the direction being taken by this once great airline. Throughout this report they are appealing for the assistance of the government and their MPs to make Air Canada a great airline once again.
There have also been complaints in the Senate with regard to the Air Canada operation. Last June a Senator formally put forward a question in the following terms;

I have also received complaints from Air Canada employees who take early retirement. A recent letter I received from one of them calls attention to conditions which exist at Dorval. The aspect he mentions concerns morale, and we all know this has a great bearing on productivity, safety and health. Most of the persons in their respective trades study and learn their jobs through courses; others have to qualify for MOT certificates. It is very demoralizing for them when someone less experienced is made a supervisor over trained men, especially when that person is brought in from an unrelated department. Some of the promotions and replacements which have taken place have led to very bad morale at the Dorval base.
The Air Canada magazine retirement list printed monthly shows that the biggest percentage of early retirements is constituted by personnel who have been moved from Winnipeg to Dorval in the last three or four years. These are mostly men with service of 25 years or more. They are taking their retirement early, many of them only in their fifties. It must involve a great loss to the company when valuable, knowledgeable men with practical experience retire early. To fill the vacancies requires men of a high technical competence.
The following is a short list of promotions and demotions which have taken place. In the parts shop, the general superintendent was replaced. The retired employee asks why. Also, the assistant superintendent was replaced. Foremen were set up over senior and more experienced personnel, a senior planner over senior and more experienced planners. In the metal shop a general foreman was appointed from employees of the personnel department. I realize how surprised my friends are, but that only shows they either have not been around here very long or that they have not been listening. In the few minutes I intend to take, I want to emphasize the importance of improving railway pensions. Though there are many facets of this question, I should like to concentrate on one area, that of the annual escalation of the pensions of railway workers already retired.
I am fully aware of the negotiations which took place last year, which began even earlier, leading to a new pension package as part of the collective agreement which is being considered now by the Hon. Emmett Hall. I am also aware that Dr. John Deutsch is a special commissioner who is looking at one aspect of pensions. But the fact is that he is looking at only one area, namely, the percentage value of the pension package agreed to in the collective bargaining in relation to the total benefits of the employees. In other words, Dr. John Deutsch has no authority under the commission given to him by the Minister of Labour to go into the broad question of Canadian National or Canadian Pacific pensions; he is looking at the one narrow aspect to which I have referred. He will simply report to the Hon. Emmett Hall as to the percentage value of that pension package, and then Mr. Hall will have to decide whether to make any adjustment in the wages to be decided by him under the terms of his appointment.
So, Mr. Speaker, any suggestion that pensions are dealt with because Dr. John Deutsch is working on the matter is false. Any suggestion that the matter I am concerned
January 8, 1974

about tonight is covered by the collective agreement is also false-because I am thinking particularly of the pensions of retired railway employees, those who are already on the retired list and are drawing their pensions.
The point that I zero in on particularly has to do with the rate of escalation which in the Canadian National set-up has for a number of years now been 2 per cent per year. I point out that even that annual escalation is made on an ad hoc basis: it has not been written into the rules and it has not been established in any way that employees can count on it from year to year. True, it has been done every year since it was started, but this is by the grace of the company.
Even more serious than the fact that the annual escalation of CNR pensions is not guaranteed is the fact that it is still limited to 2 per cent per year. Not many years ago, when the escalation of pensions first commenced, that figure of 2 per cent was established and we were stuck with it for a long time. But our efforts have not been in vain; we have succeeded in that getting that 2 per cent ceiling removed in the case of most pensions paid under the aegis of the government. For example, if a person is receiving old age security he now receives every year, not simply an increase of 2 per cent but an increase that is equal to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living. The same is true of persons in receipt of the guaranteed income supplement.
Then, again, I could mention the pensions of retired public servants. For a number of years their pension increase was at the rate of only 2 per cent per year no matter how much the cost of living went up. Their increase is now geared to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living. The same is true of retired armed forces and retired Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel. Many of those retired persons have still another grievance which I might mention in passing, namely, that they have to wait until they are 60 before getting an increase. But the point I am making is that those who get the annual increase get it at a rate equal to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living.
The same can be said of pensions paid to veterans. I am thinking both of the war disability pensions paid under the Pension Act and allowances paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Those benefits are escalated every year, not simply by 2 per cent but by the actual percentage increase in the cost of living. I point out that family allowances are in the same category now; they, too, increase not by a fixed amount but by the actual percentage increase in the cost of living.
I might even mention retired members of parliament. They have pensions and are in fact part of a preferred pension plan, although some of those who retired a number of years ago before the plan was improved do not think it is as good all that. But even they will discover this month, if they are over 60 years of age, that their pension will not increase simply by 2 per cent but will be increased by an amount equal to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living.
So I could go on, Mr. Speaker. I have not had the chance to check every last pension that is paid under government auspices, but I think I have mentioned enough of them and have studied the situation sufficiently to be able to make
Canadian National Railways
the general statement that pensions, allowances and superannuation benefits that are federal in their origin are now all in the position of being increased each year by an amount equal to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask what is wrong with railway employees, and particularly with Canadian National employees? Why are they not getting similar treatment? Actually, I am as concerned about employees who worked for the CPR as I am about those who worked for the CNR and are now retired. They are not included within the provisions of this bill, but I think they ought to be. What bothers me is that far too often, I think, does the CPR decide upon pension policy and then that company browbeats the CNR to go along with the decision it has made.
In any event, we are now dealing with a bill that grants money to Canadian National Railways and so it is to the Canadian National Railways that we must direct our fire. I contend that employees of the Canadian National Railways are, in a practical sense, just as much employees of the government of Canada as are all these other groups to which I have referred. I think it is a shame, a disgrace- perhaps even calling it a crime would not be language that is too strong-that this particular group of people who work for the government of Canada have pensions that are restricted to an annual increase of 2 per cent, whereas all the others get an increase that is equal to the actual percentage rise in the cost of living.
I see my good friend the hon. member for St. Boniface over on the other side. May I still call him the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport? I have not seen the order in council that was tabled today, so I do not know whether he was retained in that position or transferred.
