speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be unfair or untrue to say that every member of this chamber shares the sentiments just expressed by one of our more distinguished senior citizens regarding faulty management of the CNR. I think we are in agreement for a variety of reasons but, if for no other reason, because-as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-this situation has existed for a long time and it is inhuman.
Let me join in the general theme of our discussion on this amendment which relates to the faulty management of the CNR. In the few minutes available to me I should like to touch upon another dimension which in its own way is equally as irresponsible and, indeed, borders on the criminal. I refer to the area of safety on the railway. I have in mind the number of accidents which have occurred not only in rail transportation but in all forms of transportation in Canada which fall within the purview and jurisdiction of the federal authority.
Perhaps, to set the tenor of my remarks, I should emphasize that the point I want to make-I have mentioned this on a number of occasions in this chamber in recent years- relates to the very obvious conflict of interest that arises in respect of transportation accidents when the body responsible for making and enforcing regulations is also charged with the responsibility of investigating those accidents and making judgments as to their cause, liability, and so on. It is in this area that I have an interest. I will keep my remarks in context by suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members that what I am talking about is bad management. When I conclude my remarks I will place this subject in absolute perspective and in context with the amendment which is before us.
Since yesterday afternoon we have had before us the CTC report by the Railway Transport Committee entitled "Third report of the railway safety inquiry". When I refer to conflict of interest I have in mind management which permits this type of inquiry to be undertaken without any objection by a committee of the CTC. This is what I mean

when I suggest this is man's inhumanity, if you will, to man. This amounts almost to criminal action because of the failure by the commission to do something, and more often than not in this case the crime is failure to act rather than acting in a wrong way.
In August, 1970, the Railway Transport Committee, which is an arm of the regulatory body, decided to set up an inquiry into a series of train wrecks that occurred at about that time. This was a wise thing to do internally; there is no doubt about that at all. The committee decided to do this, and arbitrarily decided that as an arm of the regulatory body it was the only group competent and able to carry out this type of inquiry. I quote from the top of page 4 of their third report as follows;
-the committee decided to assign its two most senior and experienced officers with expertise in this field to the job of preparing reports on all aspects of railway operation and maintenance-
The field referred to here is that of safety. How could the two most senior people in this area properly advise their senior officials as to what is happening and what should be done internally to correct certain wrongs in respect of safety? the very fact that the decision to set up this inquiry was made in August of 1970, almost 3'/2 years ago, bears out this point. Had such an investigation been carried out by an independent commission of inquiry into these accidents on the CNR, I am sure this report would have been before the House within six months. Some 3 VS years later we still do not have the final report, and the committee has not indicated a date when it expects to submit it. All we have been told is that we may expect it some time in the future, and that is not good enough. The last people to complain about this situation are those in the management of Canadian National Railways, our national transportation system. We have not heard one word of objection and no complaint has been made. Indeed, I imagine management has welcomed this fact and has accepted it as sort of a whitewash.
When accidents occur in the transportation industry in Canada it is no longer tolerable that the regulatory body conduct its own investigations. This gives rise to a conflict of interest. I will not recite examples because I have put them on the record a number of time in recent years. How can a person working on one side of the room for perhaps most of his lifetime make an objective judgment as to safety measures or standards decided upon and put into effect by his friend working on the other side of the room? I suggest he just cannot do so.
We remain the only western nation which clings to this archaic and philosophically wrong method of investigating accidents. The CNR, Air Canada and the investigative branch of the Department of Transport have done absolutely nothing about this situation. I am not making any accusations or imputing any wrong motives to the members of that branch. Indeed, they are among the finest air accident investigators in the world: they have won several national awards for their high standards of investigative work. But the investigative body was a limb or a branch not even at arm's length of the regulatory body. For example, I wonder how many of the 13 or 14 points made by the judge in the hearing of the tragic DC-8 crash in 1970 have been fully implemented by Air Canada. We
January 8, 1974

know some of them have been implemented immediately, but I wonder if all of them have.
I am talking about the growing rate of accidents in all modes of transport-air, shipping, rail, interprovincial trucking and busing. The carnage of the highways and in the air as a result of these accidents grows every year. The amount of information made available to the public is negligible. We have not had half a dozen public inquiries into serious Canadian transportation accidents in the last 15 years. That is not good enough. What this country needs and what management groups such as CNR must do is to urge all governments to move as quickly as possible toward the establishment of a commission of inquiry removed from parliament, so that the possibility of a conflict of interest cannot arise and so that users of the national transportation system, be they Canadians, visitors to our country or exporters into our country, can use our transportation facilities with safety and to their satisfaction.
I regret the removal, for example, mentioned by an earlier speaker in this debate, of the direct control over Crown agencies, not because they should be the day to day concern of the House of Commons but because in the absence of responsible management principles in areas such as safety not even the House of Commons and not even our colleagues in the other place have any way of questioning management regarding whether the fullest means of ensuring safety in areas of transportation are being taken. I regret the loss of parliamentary control, if for no other reason than for that reason, and I think every member of this chamber should regret it. When the remotest possibility of a conflict of interest arises and the loss of life is the consequence of an accident, all of us should remember that we have sat here and done nothing.
Equally important in the management of CNR is exactly that type of body that could urge upon the government the necessity of removing from the purview of the regulatory body or agency the responsibility for investigation. With regard to air accidents in 1972, there were 155 fatalities and some 629 accidents, 83 of which were fatal. With regard to projections to the end of last year, the figures I have are to November 30 of last year and they show that there were 161 fatalities from 745 accidents.
Rail accidents are in another area of management. I know that different criteria are involved here, but how on earth can anyone expect to understand what is going on when Statistics Canada report that there were 1,922 accidents in 1970 and the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications reports that there were 4,622 in the same year? Those figures have grown to 4,818 according to the committee, and 1,963 according to Statistics Canada. Again we have a discrepancy with regard to fatalities. According to Statistics Canada, the number increased from 180 fatalities in 1970 to 226 in 1972, but the committee reports 195 in 1970 and 255 in 1972. What happened to the other 29 deaths? Is that a responsible way for the management of one of our largest conglomerates to approach the disclosure of information? It does not display much concern for the public.
Canadian National Railways
I am concerned about the disclosure of information, I am concerned about faulty management and I am concerned enough to wonder sometimes why we should sit here and give Air Canada $140 million and CNR another $100 million. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) said that they made operating profits in all but three of the last 25 years. That is fine; but I wonder about the Department of Transport through whom this august body reports to parliament. I wonder about their attitude to CNR and their obvious lack of concern for faulty or bad management. In the editorial of the Evening Patriot of December 22 the following account is to be found:
On Thursday of this week, a light civilian aircraft landed on a runway at the Charlottetown airport across the path of Eastern Provincial Airways flight 112 incoming from Montreal. This incredibly dangerous incident happened before the eyes of a startled group of passengers in the airport lounge-
The final paragraph of the editorial reads as follows:
This is the capital city of a province of Canada. We no longer live in a horse-and-buggy age. This newspaper is demanding immediate action on the part of the Department of Transport to correct this situation for the sake of the safety of all passengers who use the Charlottetown airport facilities.
What they are complaining about is the absence of a landing tower manned by somebody who says, "Come on in; it is safe to land" or, "It is safe to take off; the wind is blowing at such and such a velocity, the altimeter is reading so and so, your visibility is such and such". Those are simple safety procedures. I can understand now why the government does not give a damn about what the CNR does. I suppose a government that would permit the principal airport in a province of Canada to remain without a manned tower for safety's sake does not give a darn about what procedures are followed with respect to safety measures or investigations of accidents in any form of transportation. This is what I regret about the management of CNR, the management of Air Canada and the management of all other forms of transportation in Canada.
I regret their failure to bring pressure to bear on this government to correct the very obvious and glaring errors in our approach to safety in transportation in Canada. It is a simple thing to do. I sometimes wonder whether the government, recognizing that this is a principle which should be put into practice, is reluctant to do so because the suggestion essentially comes from an opposition member of parliament. For years they have neglected to do anything about this most serious situation.
I support the amendment of the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) because it condemns the management of the CNR. It pinpoints areas where that management has failed. I will continue to support the amendment until the management of Crown corporations like CNR and Air Canada begin to demonstrate a little more concern for the responsibilities and authority we give them rather than for mere management and the achievement of operational profits and, I might add, capital losses.
When members of management begin to demonstrate to me that they are concerned about the human aspects and are concerned about ensuring that the users of our transportation systems need not have cause to worry about the possibility of conflict of interest in the investigation of

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
accidents, then I will start to change my mind and perhaps be a little bit more willing to give the CNR the amount of money it needs. We need an independent commission of inquiry to conduct impartial accident investigations. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) agrees that we have done nothing. I leave it to him in his new appointment to face this problem and do something.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak on the subject of the railways, particularly the CNR. For the past 25 years I have observed the disintegration of CNR services. The CNR was created to provide service to the people of Canada; it was not created to ease the tax burden as a whole. Initially, many concessions were made to the railways to encourage them to build tracks across the country. In terms of real estate, those concessions are now paying off very well for them. Yet we hear the railways say they cannot haul grain, that it is not paying them to haul grain. I point out that they have an obligation to haul grain and to try to keep this country together. It is utter nonsense for them to talk in terms like that.
The CNR is an agency of the federal government and the government is certainly responsible for its actions. In this bill we find the CNR seeking money for capital expenditures, not to improve its railway services, not to slow down the disintegration of those services but to spend on other projects. It has chosen to turn its back on the tracks in order to build needles in the sky. People in railway management know that the rails are disintegrating and that they will not be able to provide service much longer. They are lagging behind in things they should be doing. They should be spending money on the repair of tracks in all parts of Canada so that the CNR can continue to provide the service which it was created to provide.
It seems that people in the CNR do the things they like to do, and any time they are met with a little competition they just ease out and let someone else take over. It is a good example for budding socialists of what happens when government shifts its responsibilities onto Crown agencies and tells them, "Run things the best you can and we will pour in all the money you need." Every year officials of the CNR come before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. They admit their failures and their faults, but then go back and continue to commit the same faults. Seemingly, it is a failure of the democratic process that these agencies increase in number, becoming more complex in their operations and thus making it more difficult for the will of the people to be carried out through their instrumentality.
There are three services that the CNR should be providing-carriage of freight, carriage of passengers and the movement of bulk commodities across Canada. But it has almost completely moved out of the freight business. One way it did this was by providing poor living accommodation for its employees. Its passenger business has gone the same way. I once came to Ottawa on the train. Most people you talk to have travelled on the train-once. They don't do it again. In fact, from the time I got on at Saskatoon until I reached Ottawa I had the impression that someone kept asking me was I not aware that I could fly and did not have to travel by train.

Now there is a failure on the part of the CNR to move bulk commodities and grain. We had an election campaign last year. We had "Build for a billion" stickers all across the Prairies. I imagine there are still a few of them around. But the very next year the Wheat Board says "we cannot fulfil contracts for grain because we cannot guarantee to get the wheat into export position." As recorded at page 84 of the minutes of the transport and communications committee of December 11 last, Mr. MacMillan said that their target for the period August 1 to December 8 was 67,628, cars and the actual supply of cars numbered 65,738. On the one hand we have the railways saying they reached their target, and on the other hand we have the minister in charge of the Wheat Board saying that they did not reach their target because cars were tied up with potash and lumber.
Then the joking Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) suggested there were too many Canadian cars in the United States and talked about sending an engine down to the United States to pick up loose Canadian cars and bring them back. When he does not know the answer to something, the Minister of Transport makes a joke. We are supposed to put up with that. We are not likely to get good performance from the CNR when we have that minister.
Of course, the Wheat Board said it disagreed with the railways. Here are two agencies of the federal government which negotiate with each other every year, yet they cannot agree on the number of boxcars over the period August 1 to December 8. Mr. Gibbings suggested in committee that the target was 61,000 cars, but only 43,000 cars were delivered. Surely to goodness we have the right to expect a better performance than that from these agencies? Are these people being paid the minimum wage so that we must accept that sort of performance from them? Surely we have the right to expect better than that from the Minister of Transport and from the minister responsible for the Wheat Board? These agencies work together all the time. They sit down together and set targets. Then they come here and report to our standing committee. Of course, they say that the language each one uses is different. The CNR is talking about car equivalents and the Wheat Board is talking about actual cars. We have all this sort of gibberish. Surely the people of Canada can expect better performance from the responsible ministers.
We are faced now with a situation where there is very little grain at the lakehead. The president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool says we are 5,000 boxcars short in Vancouver today. Next spring, when the grain is coming into the elevators, we will be back where we started, wondering what happened to the 2,000 boxcars that were supposed to solve the problem. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board, and the government, have been asked to supply more hopper cars to the railways, but we have not received any answers to our requests. Surely the government must take the matter in hand and see that the rolling-stock is provided so that grain and all other commodities in Canada can be moved.
In Saskatchewan, where I come from, we rely tremendously upon the railways. We produce more than we can use and have to export, so we depend upon the railroads. They will have to operate better in order to serve us. The
January 8, 1974

answer is not to raise the Crowsnest Pass rate. This year the railways have been able to charge what they like for lumber, but they have not provided the service required by the people in the business. They offer no guarantee to improve the service, but simply ask for more money so they can build more hotels or more towers in places like Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, the CN was created by an act of parliament. We could have another act of parliament just as easily and restructure the CNR. The people involved should be made aware of their obligations and the service that should be provided for those Canadians who need it, and we should see that they carry out their responsibilities.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to this debate very carefully for the last two days. It is a well-known fact that the railways were declared by parliament to be "works for the general advantage of Canada". I have been very surprised at what I have found since coming to Ottawa. We seem to be faced with a whole series of problems such as the failure of the government to provide auditing of both the CNR and Air Canada's financial operations. We have the problem of the annual ritual of this CNR financing act to delude the public. The financial affairs of Canada's two greatest public utilities are controlled by the government and by the government alone.
We are faced with the problem of discriminatory freight rates and the collective complaints of the western premiers that it is impossible to assess the internal operations of the CNR accurately. We are also faced with the problem of financial mismanagement of the Canadian National, its long-term debt and its loans to Air Canada. Worst of all, we are faced with the failure of this government to develop a comprehensive national transportation policy.
Mr. Speaker, I used to think that the Canadian National had a major obligation to provide service, to carry goods and passengers. In the area that I come from, passenger service is almost non-existent. We deliver grain to a line that has a 20-mile an hour speed limit and where they have been replacing an average of one railway tie per mile per year for the last eight years. In this area the Canadian National receives a subsidy of over $100 for every boxcar of grain that they haul out. That is on top of the freight rate. The boxcars that are delivered are often a disgrace. They require patching and repair by the local grain buyer before loading. The buyer is afraid to reject a car because they are so scarce that he might not get a replacement.
There is a CNR line in my area where they abandoned the last 12 or 13 miles of track to the last elevator, and now Canadian National are paying the trucking costs from the last elevator which is some 20 miles to the city of Swift Current. The transportation of grain in particular in this crop year is a complete fiasco and farm deliveries are 150 million bushels less than this time last year. The Canadian Wheat Board and the railways cannot agree on the grain targets and we still have not received any satisfaction on that question. Officials of the railway companies are questioning the Crowsnest Pass rates, and I have the uncomfortable feeling that they have had some encouragement from the Canadian Wheat Board, from the minister in
Canadian National Railways
charge of the Wheat Board or from Department of Transport officials.
Question after question remains unanswered. Is it the intention of this government to announce, some time in the near future, a comprehensive, long-range rail transportation policy which will provide not only for the effective rationalization of rail operations but also for some logical alternative to the current energy shortage? On what basis does this government justify an annual subsidization of approximately $180 million for uneconomic rail lines, when these funds could be diverted into research concerning both alternate modes of transportation and alternate fuel systems? Why has there been so little research into rail transportation in Canada? Why has there not been research by the appropriate government agencies as well as private interests? Is the lack of government support and initiative, both economically and morally, concerning rail transportation research a major reason for this unrealistic inertia?
Would it not be more economically feasible to shelve the STOL program between Montreal and Ottawa and use the money instead to modernize the already existing rail system between these two cities? By "modernize" I mean not only increasing the frequency of the number of trains between Ottawa and Montreal but also the running times of trains between these two cities. Would not the electrification of the line between Ottawa and Montreal be less expensive than the STOL program?
I should like to know this government's views concerning the use of railways as a means of long-haul passenger transportation in Canada. Have the railways seen their day in this respect? Should transportation by air be encouraged more and more as a means of long-haul passenger transportation in Canada? Many questions such as these remain unanswered.
Let us look at what our neighbours to the south are doing about rail transportation. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Wall Street Journal of December 28 which reads:
The Interstate Commerce Commission issued the nation's first set of regulations designed to force improved intercity rail-passenger service.
The rules apply to Amtrak and the railroads that run its trains,...
They mandate a nationwide, toll-free telephone reservations and information system; enough seating space to meet "normal demands" of customers seeking reservations; minimum levels for train-on-time performance, baggage delivery, train connections and station hours, and a range of other standards for food, temperature control, sleeping cars, rest rooms and drinking fountains.
The regulations take effect April 1. ICC chairman George M. Stafford said they are designed "to improve the overall quality of 'America' passenger train service and thereby make rail travel attractive, especially during the current energy crisis."
Newspaper after newspaper in the United States speaks of the updating of the transportation system in that country. According to one report, travel on Amtrak trains will go "right through the roof". Amtrak officials themselves now expect ridership to leap 30 per cent next year, double what they previously predicted. I quote once more from the Wall Street Journal of December 28:
-Amtrak has been flooded with state bids for new routes. Nebraska would like an Omaha-Kansas City train, Colorado a Denver-Kansas City route, Missouri a Kansas City-St. Louis route, and Ohio a Cincin-
9172

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
nati-Columbus-Cleveland run. "I've had to put a map on my wall showing all the inquiries and expected inquiries. It looks like a ... spider web," an Amtrak state-relations official says.
What is the general situation in Canada, Mr. Speaker? There are only two passenger rail lines in all of Canada which are not subsidized-the Quebec-North Shore-Labrador line, because it has never applied, and the CPR's Esquimalt-Nanaimo route on Vancouver Island because upon investigation it was found that the rail line had done nothing to improve its services, thus the request for application was denied. The railways need only apply once for abandonment of passenger service. Upon initial application the Canadian Transport Commission undertakes a study of the area to review the effects abandonment would have on the area. If these effects are thought to be detrimental to the population, the service is continued under a subsidy which amounts to 80 per cent of the loss claimed. In the following years an annual claim is made and audited by CTC officials. Each year over $100 million is expended in subsidies allotted to unprofitable railway services. A Canadian Transport Commission spokesman is quoted as saying that there are no passenger train lines in Canada making any money.
The main reason the abandonment procedure operates in this manner is that the 1967 National Transportation Act encourages the diversion of funds into unprofitable operations rather than into the research and development of advanced railway technology. The most logical alternative to the wasting of federal moneys on these unprofitable operations would be to divert a portion of the funds into research for more effective and efficient services. Electrification is a viable consideration. The modernization of railways, as represented by their electrification, has yet to start in Canada. Seventy per cent of gross ton-miles are generated by electric traction in West Germany, France and Japan. The capital investment required by electrification is far outweighted by the resultant service. The benefits entailed from this type of modernization include lower capital and maintenance costs of locomotives, longer life, higher availability, better adhesion, higher speed, better braking performance and superior environmental characteristics.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the railways in Canada have been declared to be works which are for the general advantage of the public of Canada. I think the taxpayer of this country is entitled to expect a better shake from the government in the matter of transportation.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating the amendments to this bill. My colleagues tell me that it does not much matter whether this bill passes or not, because CN and Air Canada will spend the money anyway. So why are we debating this bill if the money is to be spent? Is this not a mockery of parliament?
The amendment before us seeks to deny Canadian National Railways so many millions of dollars which are to be spent on the huge structure known as the tower in Toronto. I am told that the tower is two-thirds completed. If the amendment passes, will the tower stand two-thirds finished and never be completed, or will it be finished in any event? Therefore I think this debate is ridiculous. We

should pass the bill and get it over with, because the tower is three-quarters finished anyway. Let us not be stupid.
A member to my right talked about the CNR as an example of socialist inefficiency. Apparently CN service is very poor. Well, if those fellows want to talk about socialists, let me tell them some things.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: You are not a socialist, are you?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
You bet I am, and proud of it. They say that Canadian National gives poor service, that it does not do the job. I admit the service is poor and that the railway does not do its job. But the service is not as poor as the service of the CPR. Actually, it is a bit better. The previous speaker mentioned how wonderful are the railway companies in the United States, how well they are doing, and so on. Mr. Speaker, they are going bankrupt left and right and there is no end in sight to the trend of bankruptcies.
I was in Washington during the week of November 26 to November 30. I was at a dinner given in the Canadian embassy. One chap with whom I had the honour of speaking said, "You know, I was in Canada three years ago. My, you guys have a wonderful railroad service." I asked him which railroad he travelled on. He said, "It was one of those government operations." I said, "Was it the Canadian National?" He said, "Yes, that's it" Further, he said that passenger service on the Canadian National was ten times better than anything he had ever seen in the United States. So who do you believe, the man who has travelled on Canadian and American trains or the Wall Street Journal?
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said yesterday in his speech that he had fought against the concept of taking the railroad station from downtown Ottawa to the suburbs. He neglected to say that Canadian National was never in favour of the move and that the Conservative government of the day forced the move to the outskirts of Ottawa. So what are members to my right talking about?
Some complain that Canadian National Railways are getting too much into real estate. Some members have mentioned the CN tower in Toronto. I agree with some hon. members on one or two small points. For example, I do not think the Canadian National should hang on to railway rights-of-way which it secured about 40 years ago, rights-of-way on which it has no intention of building rail lines.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: It sold them in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
I am talking about the right-of-way from St. Walburg to Loon Lake. No railway line has been built. That is to say, the railway is hanging on to the choice piece of property in the village. The village is expanding. It cannot expand more because it is surrounded by an Indian reserve. There are 50 housing lots on the railroad right-of-way, but the railway says, "We do not want to give up property because some day we may build a rail line on it". Big deal! They are trying to abandon 400 miles of line in my constituency, but claim they need this property for possible future lines. That will be the day!
January 8, 1974

One of the problems with CN concerns management. Too often we have appointed to the board of directors, or to the office of vice-president or president, men who know nothing about the railroad, men who were not brought up on the railroad or know how to run one. We have tended to appoint to the big paying positions political hacks. A man may not have done too well in the House of Commons, so he is made president or vice-president of CNR.
I want to tell members to my right a little more. There is a great problem with regard to boxcars and the movement of wheat. I am concerned about the movement of grain. I understand that at the present time CNR is repairing 900 grain cars. Some of them are battered and have greatly depreciated. These repairs are being carried out in Winnipeg and somewhere in Quebec. My inquiries also indicate that Canadian Pacific is doing absolutely nothing about repairing or buying new cars. At least the CNR is making an effort.
The basis of our problems is that we expect CNR to operate like the CPR. CNR is a people's railroad: it must serve the people of Canada but not on the same basis as the CPR. This is what our party will ensure when we form the government some day.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: That will happen some day. We will operate the CNR and CPR when we take over. We will rationalize the transportation policy of this country. There will no longer be short Air Canada flights between Ottawa and Montreal. By the time a plane gets up 13,000 feet it is time to start coming down. It then takes two hours to get from Dorval to downtown Montreal. It only takes two hours to drive from here to the Queen Elizabeth Hotel. For short run passenger service trains are the only logical answer. We should forget about aeroplanes; they use a lot of energy.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Do you know where Montreal is?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Yes, I have been there a few times. There have been complaints about inadequate passenger service. I live in northern Saskatchewan. I travel from Saskatoon on the CNR passenger train. That is a good service. In southern Saskatchewan they do not have good service. That is because CPR runs through Regina. In my area we are satisfied with the passenger service.
I have read many articles and reports on state-operated railways. Some of the most efficient railways in the world today are being operated in France, Germany and Italy.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: What about Japan?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
These are state-operated railways. The taxpayer has been underwriting the losses of the CPR for the past 50 or 100 years: let us not be gullible about that. There are many railway companies in the country south of us. They are all going bankrupt. Pennsylvania went bankrupt a while ago. I guess that is a railroad called Pennsylvania. Our railroads also went bankrupt. It is up to the government of Canada to resurrect them. The government
Canadian National Railways
did not bail them out as they bailed out the shareholders, the people who had money in the railroads.
Until the government of Canada has the guts to make the railroad system a people's railroad we will not have a transportation system that will satisfy the needs of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the allocation of money to Canadian National Railways and Air Canada, and in particular on the amendments of the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) having to do with funds for hotels and towers. I wish to speak briefly about a hotel with which I am somewhat familiar. It is located in a city close to where I live, the Hotel McDonald. The hon. member mentioned that its profits are somewhat low. I know they have a manager problem. They have night managers, day managers, assistant managers, food control managers, beverage control managers, and I suspect they even have a manager who is available in case all those managers happen to be out at the same time. I am familiar with the time it had problems and ten people were fired. Another manager was hired to find out the problem. As the hon. member for Mississauga said, it is no wonder the McDonald made only $15,000 in 1971, and $31,000 in 1972 with an investment of $8.3 million. In addition, this hotel gets most of the convention traffic in the city of Edmonton.
I wish to refer for a moment to Mr. MacMillan's opening remarks when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. He said:
Our activities today include such things as telecommunications, hotels, trucking, passenger buses, marine services, real estate, industrial location, international consulting, pipeline studies, and the provision of transportation and telecommunications expertise for large-scale resource development. And, without neglecting our basic job of providing good rail transportation, we are expanding in many of these fields and looking towards other fields of diversification.
These amendments single out only two of the things in which the railways are involved, namely, hotels and towers. Air Canada has 21 vice-presidents. I wonder how many vice-presidents are necessary for CNR to handle all the diversification in which they are involved. I have no trouble in supporting these two amendments. Even though CNR has been traditionally involved in hotels, I believe these amendments point out that parliament is concerned about the diversification of the CNR into these many facets. The CNR should have to borrow the money for hotels, TV in hotels and tourist attractions in Toronto from other sources. They should be involved in the encouragement of passenger and freight service and safety as well as providing luxurious hotels and towers.
In committee I asked about the safety record of CNR. I pointed out that I understood it was poor. I received a comparison with the United States. I then pointed out that only $19 million per year was put into improving railway crossings. I stated it should be necessary to put more funds into the updating of railway crossings because 85 per cent of them are not marked with flashing lights. Perhaps this is one reason for the poor safety record of CNR. The answer I received is that it is necessary to accelerate the program but it will be necessary to substantially increase the funds available. I was told these level
26695-68i

January 8, 1974
Canadian National Railways
crossing projects have become very expensive and it will take several million dollars to update them.
The following was pointed out to me by a constituent, and I quote from his letter of July 9:
The daily passenger makes a round trip from Calgary, Drumheller, Camrose and Edmonton. This passenger train does not always blow the whistle. Now, to the best of my knowledge, the said passenger has had two accidents this year about two months apart.
One was near Edmonton where a gravel truck was hit. The other accident, I believe, was between Drumheller and Calgary. It killed all six passengers in the car. This is the CNR.
Soon after he had pointed this out to me by letter-and of course I notified the CNR-he sent me a further letter telling me that a dayliner had hit a truck and two people had been killed. So there are problems and, as my hon. friend from Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) stated, the CTC has also expressed this opinion in a report. Instead of towers, hotels and STOL aircraft providing service between Montreal and Ottawa, perhaps we should be more concerned about passenger train service. We learn that by the end of 1971 the CTC had received 69 applications for discontinuance covering virtually all passenger transportation services in Canada. The significance of this is clear. The railways are not prepared to provide any passenger service whatsoever unless subsidies are available from the government and the government is prepared to provide such subsidies in the public interest.
Another omission which concerns me is the lack of effective research. When the president of the CN was before the committee I asked why the transcontinental train only arrives on schedule 34 per cent of the time. He told me-and I was surprised at his answer-that our winter conditions made it difficult to get these trains across Canada on time. The biggest problem, apparently, was the cold-the icy winds that affect the running of the trains. I asked whether any research had been carried out to overcome this problem, perhaps through the better heating of these cars. Apparently none has been carried out up to this time. I believe the railway should become more deeply involved in researching better means of transporting people across the country.
These, Mr. Speaker, are some of the reasons I feel we should support the amendment before us. I feel the CNR should get away from all this diversification and become more concerned in the handling of freight and passengers. That was its business to start with, and it should continue to be so.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall, of course, ask hon. members to support the amendments before them. At the same time I should like to make a few remarks of my own about both Canadian National and Air Canada. Each of these concerns is a public utility in the true sense of the word. A public utility is created, not as an occasion for self-aggrandizement, not to build empires but to serve the public where it is either impossible or undesirable for private enterprise to do so. And may I say to my demi-semi, pretend-socialist friends-if there are any of them here-that I have not come here to sing the praises of the Canadian Pacific, whose performance I

believe to be as abominable as that of any other transportation company in this country. After having been deeded half the country to provide transportation where it was needed, they goofed, they blew it, they built themselves into a giant multinational corporation, one could almost call it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Multicorporate corporation, perhaps?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Yes, multicorporate corporation, as someone near me says. I would suppose that in the case of Canadian National it would devote itself to the movement of goods from point to point in this country where it was necessary to do so. Instead, what did we see in the annual report? We see not only luxury hotels and communications towers, but satellites, trucking companies and Lord knows what else.
What we do not see is much evidence of the successful movement of people and the moving of goods such as grain and lumber from place to place in this country. And there are people who are being very badly hurt by this failure. In fact, because of the policy of the railroads, which it pleases their highly-paid bosses to call rationalization, which usually means screwing the people in one way or another, entire towns have disappeared from the west. Anyone who knows the Prairies can confirm this. But they do not care about that. In the financial statement we read that in 1972 Canadian National carried record amounts of traffic, earned the highest revenues in its history and "continued its steady improvement in over-all financial results which has taken place in recent years". Then the company's president, Mr. MacMillan, says at the conclusion of his commentary:
The management and board of directors of Canadian National look forward to a continuation of the steady progress toward planned objectives which has taken place in recent years. They recognize the contribution made to this progress by the thousands of men and women who make up Canadian National-
And so on. Then they tell us they lost $17.8 million. I grant you that is a heck of a lot better than the $67.5 million they lost in 1960, but if this is their best year, by my reckoning it is going to take them until 1980 to break even at the rate they are going. That is not what I would call running a company very well.
As to Air Canada, may I say I have travelled hundreds of thousands of miles in aircraft of every conceivable kind, to almost every point in this world, over the last 20 years. I want to tell hon. members I have had better service on Air Congo than I have had on a great many Air Canada flights. Begin with the necessary task of making a reservation in Ottawa to go to Montreal, Toronto, Chicago or wherever. Here we are, in the capital of Canada, the seat of parliament. When ones phones for a reservation, who picks up the phone? Somebody in Montreal. It used to be one could telephone to the airport and some friendly person would say, "Better hang back and not spend the money on a cab to come out here, because the whether is bad and the plane may not get off the ground." You cannot do that now, because in Montreal they don't know what is happening here in Ottawa and they seem to have no way of finding out. Indeed, you are lucky if you can find someone to answer the phone in the first place. But if you surmount that obstacle, if you get a reservation and find there is a reasonable probability that the plane will take
January 8, 1974

off, you board the aircraft. If you are only going to Toronto or Montreal it is not very important, but if you are going out west, as a great many members of this House have to do-

The real responsibility lies over there in the empty pew which is sometimes occupied by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF RAIL LINE RELOCATION IN VIEW OF ENERGY CRISIS
URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF RAIL LINE RELOCATION IN VIEW OF ENERGY CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 21 I directed a question to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) concerning whether or not the minister was now considering increasing the 50 per cent federal government cost-sharing formula for rail line relocation in Canadian cities in an effort to promote intercity rail transit in co-operation with the municipalities and provinces.
As could have been expected, the answer from the minister was uninformative. He said that my question would be best answered when legislation is introduced. One has to wonder, however, when any legislation concerning this subject will be forthcoming from the government. In view of the energy crisis, it is indeed surprising that there is no federal policy regarding intercity rail transportation or on any means of urban transportation, for that matter.
Actually, the question I directed to the minister concerns two interrelated subjects: rail line relocation and intercity rail transportation, which may fall more under the realm of the Department of Transport than the Department of Urban Affairs. Many Canadian cities are planning to relocate railway tracks away from downtown areas, thus freeing large amounts of property for urban development. One tremendous advantage inherent in such a relocation is that connections from these could provide a means of transporting people to and from the inner city. With the possiblity of fuel shortages in Canada this winter and the prospect that these shortages may extend for some time to come, it seems imperative that the government give consideration to this and other suggestions which might improve intercity transportation as a means of conserving energy.
Members of this House are only too familiar with those problems which have arisen and will continue to arise from the energy crisis. Shortages of oil and gasoline necessitate that people be encouraged to leave their automobiles at home and use public modes of transport wherever possible. The best way to encourage such a transformation in the public's attitude is by developing public transportation systems which are both more efficient and economical than the private automobile.
Technology has provided us with such rapid transit systems. However, the federal government has done little to improve the current situation. It gives no leadership and has no real policy. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) summed up the government's attitude regarding urban transportation very well when on December 21 he declared:
We cannot change these things overnight.
The minister added:
There is no doubt this is something that we would like to do and we will do it wherever possible.
The question, of course, is when? I am no expert on the subjects of transportation and energy, but one does not need to have any particular expertise in these fields to realize that Canada, like other countries, has serious petroleum shortages and inadequate urban transportation

facilities. The thing that makes us unique is that we do not even have a coherent set of policies to deal with these problems.
One example of the way in which rapid transit lines could be added to existing or relocated corridors can be seen in a proposal by the Metro Toronto Transportation Commission. A study by the commission and Canadian Pacific Railway shows that the Canadian National main line corridor through east-end Toronto and Scarborough could have a 20-mile long, rapid transit line added to it at a reasonable cost. This line would provide transit for thousands daily and at the same time ease gas shortages and relieve inner-city traffic congestion and pollution. It is proposals such as this that the government should now be considering for all of Canada's urban regions, not just for some.
The federal government's decision, announced on Monday, to provide a $10 million grant to launch a province-operated commuter rail service between Richmond Hill and Toronto's Union Station is a step in the right direction. However, it should be noted that this grant, which will provide long rail service, marks only the first time that the senior level of government has directly financed a commuter service in Canada.
If the federal government is really serious about the need for public transit as an alternative to the automobile, why is it not supplying more money and leadership to the provinces to help speed the provision of new transportation services? In the city of Ottawa, at least, what the government appears to be doing is encouraging people to bring their cars into the core area. I refer to the Department of Public Works and its intention to construct a mammoth underground parking garage in the heart of the downtown area. This will encourage public employees to bring their cars to work rather than seek out public transportation. The logic escapes me.
Logic is what the United States has been using for the past several years in developing policies to deal with urban congestion and pollution. Like us, they have a long way to go, but they do have a head start on most countries. Long before the advent of the energy crisis, the Americans were formulating long-range urban transit policy. The federal government has provided the initiative and the majority of funds which have enabled governments to come to grips with the problem. Instead of building more freeways, they are building more buses and commuter trains. In these regions, particularly New York and New Jersey, new public transportation networks are now being tested as more and more motorists are opting for buses and, to a lesser extent, trains because of high fuel costs. The U.S. government's foresight is now paying off. This is an example we should have followed. I should also mention the fact that with the serious petroleum shortages, the United States is bringing back transcontinental railways in a big way. Railways once again will be trafficking large numbers of people across the country and across the states.
We in Canada should also look to the past for solutions for the future. The railway was responsible for opening up this country and in no small way has contributed toward our development and prosperity. It is perhaps time to resurrect the locomotive and to once again utilize it as a
January 8, 1974

means of ferrying persons across the provinces and across Canada. Such a revitalization of our rail lines would provide Canadians with an alternative means of transportation over relatively long distances, to say nothing of the savings in petroleum.
The passenger services currently being provided by our two national railways are at present neither efficient nor economical and do not operate on a sufficient scale to handle large numbers of people. This situation should be changed. Our railways should be encouraged to expand their passenger operations and lower their fares. As in the case in the United States, the federal government could provide subsidies to the companies to finance such an expansion. Perhaps then Canadians would leave their cars at home when travelling long distances.
In conclusion, then, I believe it is time the government got around to formulating a policy to deal with inner-city transportation. One means of providing a better urban transit system might be via rail lines connected to relocated corridors; but the actual mode chosen is not really that important. As well, the government should consider reviving railways throughout the country. What is important, though, is that something be done soon to deal with the problems which are arising. However, based on what we have seen thus far in the way of policy, I am not optimistic.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN FEDERAL SHARE OF COST OF RAIL LINE RELOCATION IN VIEW OF ENERGY CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to suggest that the government consider amending a proposed costsharing formula on legislation yet to be introduced in this House, although it will be soon, is to ask for a hypothetical response to a hypothetical situation. There is nothing to indicate that the proposed 50 per cent federal cost-sharing in railway relocation projects is not adequate. Moreover, to suggest that the cost-sharing be increased to promote intercity rail transit is to miss entirely the main purpose of the railway relocation legislation.
The proposed measure is intended for intracity, not intercity, application. It is designed, as will be readily apparent when the bill is introduced, to apply to cities where obsolete or underused railway facilities-tracks, yards, terminals-are formidable obstacles to planned and orderly urban development. Essential intercity lines will not be reduced in capacity or efficiency. The provisions in the railway relocation legislation are intended to modify the flow of traffic on lines in cities or to relocate lines entirely in accordance with urban plans formulated by the provinces and their municipalities.
Where a rail line is relocated, the property thus vacated may be put to any number of uses in accordance with the priorities established by such plans. These priorities can include the provision of improved and expanded rapid transit facilities in cities. Railway rights-of-way will, in many cases, provide excellent corridors for rapid public transit systems. It is our hope, in view of the energy crisis and for environmental considerations generally, that the municipalities will give top priorities to rapid transit systems in their urban plans prepared for railway relocation.
Of much more potential importance for intercity transit is the national transportation development corporation which the minister proposed, on behalf of the government, last October in Edmonton at the second and highly suc-
Adjournment Debate
cessful trilevel conference. He stated at the time that the federal government was making the proposal contingent on the kind of response obtained from the provinces. I can report that officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Transport and officials responsible for urban affairs have since been seeking the views of the provinces on the desirability of such a national corporation, and everywhere that response has been positive. Such a national agency will help marshall our resources to the task of meeting current and future needs in public transportation and will go some way to meeting the further demands created by the energy situation.
The need for such an agency is obvious, both on economic grounds as well as in the light of emerging energy needs. The domestic market for public transportation systems will amount to at least $5 billion over the next two decades, and we have the opportunity now to develop an integrated public transportation system that will meet, in an energy conserving way, the transit needs generated by large cities and small cities, as well as among cities.
I would like to remind hon. members also that the federal government has been carefully examining its overall role in urban transportation as was outlined in the last throne speech, and it will consult the provinces on this when the examination has been concluded. It is prepared to do this to improve and strengthen the urban environment for the future as well as to meet more pressing current needs as illustrated by the energy situation.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-TRANSPORTING OF CHILEAN REFUGEES TO CANADA BY GOVERNMENT PLANE-NUMBER INVOLVED-SCREENING-GRANTED OF LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
IMMIGRATION-TRANSPORTING OF CHILEAN REFUGEES TO CANADA BY GOVERNMENT PLANE-NUMBER INVOLVED-SCREENING-GRANTED OF LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 30, 1973, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) announced measures to assist Chilean refugees wishing to come to Canada. At that time the minister announced that in line with Canada's ongoing refugee program, the government would relax selection criteria, would accelerate immigration processing, provide language training and job placement services, assistance to cover transportation costs, financial assistance to provide for accommodation, winter clothing and other such special support to facilitate early establishment. The minister at that time said that as of that date 20 people had arrived in Canada, 50 had received their visas and the applications of 125 others were being processed as quickly as possible.
On December 21, 1973, about one month after his initial announcement to the House, the minister further announced that applications respecting approximately 1,400 persons had been received. He said that 184 visas had been issued and up to 213 additional visas could be issued once applicants had responded to the request that they come forward for their medical examinations. The minister went on to say that all applications received as of that date ought to be completed by January 31, 1974, with many being completed before the end of December, 1973. Well, Mr. Speaker, to date no refugees have landed in Canada since the minister's first announcement of November 30, 1973.

January 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
There are four groups of persons in Chile who have requested the aid of the Canadian government in leaving that country. These include Chileans who have sought refuge in the Canadian embassy; those who are seeking entry to Canada through normal, but relaxed immigration procedures; another group who are hiding in Santiago and are being hunted by the military junta; and finally those refugees, Chilean and non-Chilean, who are presently sheltered in six specially created United Nations refugee camps. By way of clarification it should be noted that those who have applied for visas on a normal basis have done so with a view to bettering their personal economic positions, as many have lost their jobs since the junta takeover. The large majority of these people have no political problems with the ruling military. On the other end of the spectrum, those who are in hiding have little or no hope of escape. They are in hiding and we do not know who they are or where they are.
The last group, those who are being cared for under the United Nations refugee program, is the group which both needs and at the same time can benefit from the minister's announced accelerated immigration program. United Nations figures of December 27 showed that 509 refugees were in camps on that day, 1,147 foreigners were on UN lists but living in the city, 123 in embassies and 23 in prison.
The minister's statement in the House that Canada was expanding its aid to refugees created a good deal of optimism and hope among UN officials and the refugees. But in actual practice the announced policy was not much relaxed, and on the contrary was found to be very strict. There were lengthy interviews, first about professional capacity, then questioning about political ideology and party affiliation, followed by medical examinations, a check-out with Ottawa and a wait of several weeks. Some later received curt, two-paragraph letters, of which I have a copy here, affirming rejection by Canada because "your admittance to Canada would be contrary to the public interest of the Canadian people." As a matter of fact, the situation has become so confusing and contradictory that Mr. Ernest Schlatter, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in Santiago, directed a letter to the Canadian ambassador in Chile, Mr. Ross, on December 28 complaining of Canada's policy in the UN operation.
Three common complaints from UN refugee camps have been that the Canadian immigration officials presume the clients to be guilty as criminal terrorists until proven innocent. The refugees have also spoken bitterly of police-type interrogation. Thirdly, the manner in which the Canadian officials have gone about assisting these refugees appears contrary to what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in his statement referred to as humanitarian considerations. The minister has not cleared up to my satisfaction the disposition of the refugees in the UN camps who have applied for entry to Canada. For example, we do not know how many from the UN camps have applied to come to Canada and what their status will be if the UN camps are closed as scheduled on February 3.
The minister has obfuscated the whole issue by quoting regular immigrant concerns about Canada's winter weather and by using meaningless phrases such as "importing

revolution," "real refugees," "revolutionaries in masquerade" and his classic statement that "all 124 immigrants are clean." Who, in heaven's name, does the minister think overthrew the democratically elected government? The terrorists and revolutionaries are in the military junta, not in the refugee camps. Why does the government regard the Latin-American refugee who has taken a stand against an oppressive, dictatorial, guerrilla regime as a criminal terrorist and not a freedom fighter, a patriot striving to build a world of justice and decency?
In recognizing the military junta diplomatically, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) announced that such recognition did not imply agreement with the junta. Yet his colleague the Minister of Manpower and Immigration appears not to have understood this, for he seems to regard it as his duty to hand over those refugees to the illegal junta, those who have most opposed the junta and who have most to fear at the hands of the military. I cannot help but feel that in the minister's view General Pinochet could fulfil the qualifications he has made necessary for the refugees. I am sure the minister could find him "clean."

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-NEGOTIATIONS WITH MARITIME EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATION ON GUARANTEEING OF LOANS
LABOUR CONDITIONS-NEGOTIATIONS WITH MARITIME EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATION ON GUARANTEEING OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a few words to the parliamentary secretary tonight arising out of a situation started many months ago on the Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec docks with regard to early retirement and an alleged undertaking by the government of Canada to guarantee full employment for the workers. I hope I have not misquoted the minister on this.
On two occasions, first on December 10 and again yesterday, I asked questions of the minister relating to the intentions of the government with respect to the guaranteeing of certain loans incurred by the Maritime Employ-
January 8, 1974

ers' Association to effect the early retirement of slightly over 500 waterfront workers in those three ports. The minister indicated to me on one occasion that he did not really know what I was talking about, and then he recalled that there was a guarantee to assist these people. Yesterday he was not certain what had happened. He was vague about it and indicated that he would try to find out something for me for today.
What we are talking about is the underwriting of loans of approximately $12 million for the Maritime Employers' Association, which is essentially a private group representing private industry and private interests based in Montreal but in fact representing east coast ports as well. I am concerned that a deal was made some time ago. I cannot imagine the Royal Bank of Canada or the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce extending to the Maritime Employers' Association something like $9 million or $10 million on the basis of the figures which in less than eight or nine months had proven to be deficient, so I must conclude that some other assurance was given to the banks. There must have been an undertaking given to the banks by the government that it would do everything in its power to effect full employment; that is, a guarantee of work through all these three ports. That is the only way I can imagine the banks would lend that amount of money to the Maritime Employers' Association.
I am sure the government at the time did not in deed or in word, maybe by implication but not by indication, guarantee the loan to the Maritime Employers' Association which is virtually on the brink of bankruptcy: they cannot meet their commitments to the banks.
I have before me a copy of the proceedings of a meeting of the Maritime Employers' Association held in Montreal on Thursday, December 13, at 2.30 p.m. This copy was distributed on December 19, 1973. I want to read one or two parts of this extract. We are dealing here with the report of A. E. Masters, president of MEA, to member companies. This company represents employers such as Atlantic Container Line (Canada) Ltd., Cast North America Limited, Clarke Transportation Canada Ltd., Federal Commerce and Navigation Co. Ltd., Kerr Steamships (Canada) Limited, Montreal Shipping Company Ltd., and so on. I think we all know their names.
In that report to the members, Mr. Masters deals with the total cost of the early retirement program, which was to run about $7 million originally and was financed by the Royal Bank and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce on the basis of cargo projection flows starting in May. These projections have now proved deficient. He deals with the three ways in which that deficiency occurred. There was a decline in cargo handled at the three river ports. The cargo shift from bulk to mechanized methods was taking place at a more rapid rate than had been anticipated and, finally, productivity had increased. That is fine and probably absolutely accurate. What concerns me has to do with the following part of the report which I now quote:
Your board is meeting with officials of the federal government in the Departments of Finance, Treasury Board and Transport immediately after this meeting with a view to finalizing the refinancing of your association's loans.
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Masters then instructed directors of MEA not to ask questions, not to discuss this because meetings were to take place that very afternoon. I am concerned about the impact on the port of Halifax of the 75-cent per ton cargo assessment put on just a few days ago to help offset pension and administration costs. We are concerned about this. Mr. Masters told the meeting not to make a fuss, not to make a noise because they were going to get the federal government to underwrite the loan, so that the cargo assessment will not have to go up for the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. The people of Halifax are understandably concerned.
I am concerned about the confusion and about what the government intends to do. Will it guarantee the loans and permit MEA to function for a month or two after the loans have been guaranteed, and then simply let them fold their tents, declare to the banks their inability to meet the loan and let the Canadian taxpayer pick up the tab? On the one hand there is increased assessment in Halifax and there is increased assessment in the port of Saint John. This will come about quickly. I hope this evening the hon. member who acted previously as parliamentary secretary can tell us of the intentions of the government with respect to these loans.
Is the government to guarantee these loans? Are we in danger of having to repay the loans to the banks? If so, what compensation is to be offered to the ports of Vancouver, Halifax, Saint John, New Brunswick, etc., and to other ports? Finally, I am concerned about the attitude of the Department of Transport, the National Harbours Board and what-have-you about the establishment of the Maritime Employers' Association in the port of Halifax, as that port can operate at a fraction of the cost which is now being charged against administration in Montreal. I know the hon. member will do his best to answer these questions. I suggest to him that his failure to do so tonight will have me on my feet again before the House adjourns.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-NEGOTIATIONS WITH MARITIME EMPLOYERS' ASSOCIATION ON GUARANTEEING OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) yesterday, as recorded at pages 9014 and 9015 of Hansard, answered in a clear manner matters raised by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). The Maritime Employers' Association is a corporation incorporated under part II of the Canada Corporations Act that represents some 85 operators who employ International Longshoremen's Association labour in the major eastern Canadian ports. There are several separate labour agreements, one of which is for the three St. Lawrence River ports of Quebec, Trois-Rivieres and Montreal, for a three-year period ending December 31, 1974.
Difficulty was experienced in the early stages of this contract due to changing cargo patterns, including the high level of containerization and diversion to other ports and the ILA strike in these ports in 1972, finally settled by an act of parliament and by arbitration which cost MEA a great deal of money to support a wage-guarantee program. In May of 1973 a reduction of some 550 men in the work force was accomplished for which MEA borrowed $7.2 million with an undertaking from NHB that the matter would be brought to the attention of the government if results showed that conventional financing was too great a burden for MEA. This present recommendation is there-

January 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
fore in fulfilment of that undertaking. The repayment program for these funds has not been met and cannot be met within the current labour agreement.
The NHB has proposed to the government that some arrangements be made to guarantee bank loans incurred by MEA for the purpose of the early retirement program for surplus longshoremen. This will remain an MEA obligation entirely and will be repaid out of MEA charges made at Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec.
There is no relationship between the MEA labour contract in these three St. Lawrence ports and the east coast ports. These are completely separate contracts and neither Halifax nor Saint John could be involved. Funds for each port in the NHB system are kept separate and distinct, and funds from Saint John and Halifax could not be used to pay any obligations in the St. Lawrence ports.
The basis of the funds to support this guarantee is reserved funds invested in government bonds from the three St. Lawrence ports out of prior years' profitable port operations. In the event that the government was ever called on to make good such a guarantee, these reserve funds would be made available by the NHB for this purpose. These total now about $30 million. There are no similar funds of any kind in the port of Halifax, and in fact the government was required to provide $1 million in the 1973 estimates to cover the operating loss of that port. There are only about $2 million of similar funds in the port of Saint John, and the NHB has pledged that this will be used for capital improvements in the port. The government has not yet completely reviewed the NHB proposal, so detailed comments are rather premature.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
